_comment: Layers of meaning: short notes on one passage, from the plain meaning outward.
section: law-history, prophets-poetry, jesus or letters-revelation, the group a passage is listed in.
kind: plain meaning, quotation, allusion, wordplay, name meaning, pattern, irony, fulfillment or setting.
strength: widely agreed (the Bible itself, a BSB footnote, or words the build can check), commonly held (an openly licensed source in the repo), or some interpreters.
refs: passages the layer rests on. words: Strong's keys the build looks for in those verses, so readers can tap them.
evidence: where a claim comes from (a lexicon, a manuscript, a commentary) and detail the note has no room for, shown at the Deep level. Keep text to 300 characters and evidence to 400.
Any quotation of four or more words must match the BSB in one of the layer's refs or the passage itself.
reviewed_by: the people who checked the entry. Entries nobody has reviewed are drafts and stay out of the published data; ATLAS_LAYER_DRAFTS=1 make data includes them for a local preview.
atlas build checks every rule and stops at the first error.

passages.saying: the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God shapes the first human from the soil and gives him life with His own breath. Human life is both earthy and God-given.

In Hebrew the man is adam and the ground is adamah: the earthling is named after the earth he came from. The pun runs through the story: there was no adam to work the adamah (2:5), and after the fall he will return to the adamah he was taken from (3:19).
Paul quotes this verse, "The first man Adam became a living being," and sets beside it "the last Adam," Christ, who does not only receive life but gives it.
Paul calls Adam "a pattern of the One to come" (the Greek word is typos, a type). As one man brought death to all, one man brings life to all.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) cites Genesis 2:7 for this verb in the Greek Old Testament
layers.text: After rising, Jesus "breathed on" His disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." The verb appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and it is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7. A new creation begins with a new breath.

passages.saying: He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, BDB, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, classic commentaries, M. H. Woudstra's article on Genesis 3:15, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, Irenaeus and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God curses the serpent that deceived the woman and declares lasting hostility between it and the woman, and between their offspring. Her seed will strike the serpent's head; the serpent will strike his heel.

layers.evidence: The count of four uses of shuph is from STEPBible TAHOT; the meaning from TBESH. The NET Bible notes point out that some translations use two different verbs here and so hide the repetition.
layers.text: "Crush" and "strike" are one Hebrew verb, shuph, found only four times in the Old Testament. Some translations hide the repetition. Both sides strike, but not in the same place: the heel, or the head, where a blow can kill.

layers.evidence: BDB: zera can mean a single descendant or many. The links to Genesis 4:25, 22:18 and 2 Samuel 7:12 follow OpenBible.info cross-references.
layers.text: "Seed" (zera) can mean one descendant or many, and the verse goes on with a singular "He." Scripture keeps tracing this seed: Seth is "another seed in place of Abel," and zera is the "offspring" promised to Abraham and the "descendant" promised to David.

layers.evidence: The Septuagint of Genesis 3:15 has autos (masculine) after sperma (neuter). M. H. Woudstra, Calvin Theological Journal 6 (1971), thinks the translators felt the personal reference was strong. The NET Bible notes say the Hebrew singular may simply agree with a collective noun.
layers.text: The Greek Old Testament uses a masculine "He" (autos), though its word for seed is neuter. One scholar thinks the translators heard one person here; others note that the Hebrew "He" may simply match "seed" as a word for a group.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Meyer and the Cambridge Bible on Romans 16:20 all point back to Genesis 3:15. The Greek verb, syntribo, means to shatter or crush (TBESG).
layers.text: Paul echoes the verse: "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet." Commentators widely hear Genesis 3:15 here. The feet are the believers' own: the victory of the woman's seed is shared with His people.

layers.evidence: Commentaries on Revelation 12:9 and 12:17 (Bible Hub) and OpenBible.info cross-references link these verses to Genesis 3:15.
layers.text: Revelation names the serpent: the "ancient serpent called the devil and Satan." The dragon goes "to make war with the rest of her children," literally the rest of her seed (sperma). The whole cast of Genesis 3:15 returns in John's vision.

layers.evidence: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 3:15 promises a remedy for the heel in the days of King Messiah (Etheridge's English, Sefaria). Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.21.1, about AD 180. The NET Bible note says Christians since Irenaeus have called the verse the protevangelium, the first announcement of the gospel, but reads its verbs as ongoing hostility.
layers.text: An old Aramaic paraphrase links the heel's healing to King Messiah, and since the second century Christians have seen Christ, "born of a woman," here. Some scholars read the grammar as lasting hostility, and the New Testament never quotes the verse directly.

passages.saying: The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, BDB, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah, classic commentaries and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God looks with favor on Abel's offering, not Cain's. Warned that sin is crouching at his door, Cain kills his brother anyway. When he asks, "Am I my brother’s keeper?" God answers that the blood itself is crying out.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible notes point out the sound play on Cain and hear in Abel's name a hint of his early death. TBESH glosses hevel as breath. BDB doubts the link and suggests the name may come from a word for son.
layers.text: Cain (qayin) sounds like Eve's "I have brought forth" (qaniti). Abel is hevel, "breath," the word Ecclesiastes uses for "futility," and some hear in it a hint of his early death. Others doubt that link and suggest a word for "son."

layers.evidence: Teshuqah occurs only in Genesis 3:16, 4:7 and Song of Solomon 7:10 (STEPBible TAHOT); meanings from TBESH. The Cambridge Bible on Genesis 4:7 calls the phrasing identical to 3:16.
layers.text: God's warning to Cain repeats His words to Eve: "Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you" becomes "it desires you, but you must master it." Same rare noun, teshuqah (desire), found only three times; same verb, mashal (rule).

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (Sefaria), paraphrased. BDB explains the plural of dam as blood in quantity or blood shed by violence.
layers.text: "Blood" is plural here, literally "bloods." Early rabbis read it as Abel's blood and the blood of all the descendants he would have had. Lexicons explain the plural as blood shed by violence, so this is a traditional reading, not the plain sense.

layers.evidence: The Greek verb for speaking is laleo in both verses (TAGNT, TBESG). Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible and Vincent's Word Studies on Hebrews 12:24 draw the contrast between vengeance and mercy.
layers.text: Hebrews says Abel "still speaks, even though he is dead," and that believers have come "to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel." Commentators draw the contrast: Abel's blood cried for vengeance, Christ's speaks mercy.

Jesus names Abel first in a long line of murdered righteous people, "from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah," and John holds Cain up as a warning: "Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother."

passages.saying: May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, classic older commentaries named under each note and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Lamech names his son Noah, hoping he will bring relief from working the cursed ground. When the earth is "full of violence," Noah finds favor with the LORD, builds the ark, and comes through the flood with his family.

layers.evidence: TBESH glosses Noah as rest. The Cambridge Bible on Genesis 5:29 calls the explanation a play on the general likeness of sound. Itstsavon occurs only in Genesis 3:16, 3:17 and 5:29 (STEPBible TAHOT).
layers.text: Noah (noach) means "rest," and Lamech explains the name with nacham, "comfort," which only sounds like it. His word for "toil," itstsavon, appears only here and in the curse on Eve and Adam (3:16-17).

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 6:8 notes that chen reverses the letters of Noah's name. Word meanings from TBESH.
layers.text: The comfort verb turns to grief: "the LORD regretted that He had made man" (nacham again). Then the story turns on one line: "Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD." Favor is chen, Noah's two Hebrew letters reversed (נח, חן).

layers.evidence: The dove's rest is manoach. TBESH glosses nichoach as soothing. The Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 8:21 hears in it an allusion to Noah's name.
layers.text: The flood ends in rest-words: the ark "came to rest" (nuach), the dove "found no place to rest," and Noah's offering is a "pleasing aroma," literally a soothing one (nichoach), perhaps a play on his name. Then God says, "Never again will I curse the ground."

layers.evidence: TBESH and the Cambridge Bible: tevah is used only of Noah's ark and Moses' basket. Keil and Delitzsch on Exodus 2:3 think the word was probably chosen to call Noah's ark to mind.
layers.text: The word for the ark, tevah, is used only for Noah's ark and for baby Moses' basket. His mother "coated it with tar and pitch" and set it in the Nile, where Pharaoh had ordered Hebrew sons thrown. Some think the word was chosen to recall Noah's ark.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) explains antitypos in 1 Peter 3:21 as the reality of which the type is the copy.
layers.text: Jesus says the Son of Man will come "as it was in the days of Noah." Peter says eight souls "were saved through water," and "this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you." "Symbolizes" is antitypos: baptism is the reality the flood pictured.

passages.saying: That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, classic commentaries, Michelle Knight's blog post on Babel, Gregory of Nazianzus and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: After the flood, people who share one language build a city with "a tower that reaches to the heavens" to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. The LORD confuses their language and scatters them anyway.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on Genesis 11:9 gives the Babylonian meaning, gate of God. TBESH glosses Babel as confusion by mixing.
layers.text: The text explains the name by a pun on balal, "confused." In Babylonian, bab-ili meant "gate of God," but in Hebrew Babel sounds like confusion. The city that called itself God's gate is remembered for scrambled speech.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Genesis 11:7 call God's words an ironic imitation of the builders; Ellicott sees irony in God taking up the phrase they used twice. Havah from TBESH.
layers.text: The builders say "Come" (havah) twice: "Come, let us make bricks" and "Come," they said, "let us build." God answers in kind: "Come, let Us go down and confuse their language." Commentators hear irony: God takes up their own words.

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible on Genesis 12:2 tells readers to contrast 11:4. TBESH glosses Shem as name; Michelle Knight (on David B. Capes's blog A Word in Edgewise) points out the Shem link.
layers.text: Babel's builders want to "make a name for ourselves"; one chapter later God promises Abram, "I will make your name great." A great name is given, not seized. Between the two stories runs the family line of Shem, whose name means "name."

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG): in the Greek Old Testament syncheo stands for balal, Babel's verb. The Septuagint also calls the city Synchysis, Confusion. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 41.16 (On Pentecost).
layers.text: At Pentecost the crowd "came together in bewilderment," each hearing "his own language." Behind "bewilderment" is syncheo, the Greek Old Testament's verb for Babel's confusion. An early Christian writer saw one Spirit bringing the languages back into harmony.

layers.evidence: Hebrew safah (lip, language), shem (name) and puts (scatter), as tagged in STEPBible TAHOT. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Zephaniah 3:9 read the verse as a reversal of Babel.
layers.text: Zephaniah promises Babel undone: God will "restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD," and His "scattered people" will bring offerings. Lip (Babel's word for language), name and scattered all come from Genesis 11.

passages.saying: and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, BDB, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Matt Champlin's Themelios article, classic commentaries and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God calls Abram to leave his country and his father's household for a land He will show him, and promises him a great nation, a great name, and a blessing that will reach "all the families of the earth."

layers.evidence: Matt Champlin, Themelios 42.1, counts both and quotes James McKeown, who calls Genesis 12 the turning point from cursing to blessing. Word data from STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH.
layers.text: Before Abram the heavy word is "cursed" (arar), five times: the serpent, the ground, Cain, the ground again, and Canaan. Now God speaks blessing five times in two verses. The story turns from curse to blessing.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from TBESH. Paul quotes Genesis 17:5 in Romans 4:17; the father of us all is his own line in 4:16.
layers.text: Later God renames him. Abram, "exalted father," becomes Abraham, father of a multitude, "for I have made you a father of many nations." Paul quotes the line and calls Abraham "the father of us all," of everyone who shares his faith.

layers.evidence: TBESG: proeuangelizomai, to announce good news beforehand, used only in Galatians 3:8. Ellicott and Meyer note that Paul joins Genesis 12:3 to 18:18. The NET Bible note says the Hebrew could also mean will bless themselves; the Septuagint, like Paul, reads it as passive.
layers.text: Paul says Scripture "foretold the gospel to Abraham": "All nations will be blessed through you." "Foretold the gospel" is one Greek word, found only here. Paul's "all nations" comes from Genesis 18:18; this verse has "all the families."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on 1 Kings 4:20 reads it as the promise of countless descendants (Genesis 22:17) fulfilled. Peter quotes the promise to Abraham in Acts 3:25.
layers.text: Near: by Solomon's day Israel was "as numerous as the sand on the seashore," as promised (22:17). Far: the blessing for all families comes in Christ, first to Israel, Peter says, and then "to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus," as Paul puts it.

layers.evidence: BDB: zera can mean a single descendant or many.
layers.text: Paul presses the word: the promise says "to your seed," not "to seeds," meaning One, who is Christ. Zera can mean one or many, and Paul uses both senses, ending the chapter: "if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed."

passages.saying: God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, BDB, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Targum Onkelos and classic commentaries.

layers.text: God promised a son to Abraham, who was about a hundred, and to Sarah, who was ninety and had never had a child. Both laughed at the thought. Then Sarah bore a son "at the very time God had promised," and Abraham named him Isaac.

layers.evidence: TBESH and BDB: Isaac means he laughs. The NET Bible notes on 21:6 say Sarah's words make a last, joyful play on the name: literally, God has made laughter (tsechoq) for me, and all who hear will laugh (yitschaq). Her laughter is now joy, not doubt.
layers.text: Isaac, yitschaq, means "he laughs," and God Himself chose the name. Abraham laughed at the promise; Sarah denied it, "I did not laugh," and the LORD said, "but you did laugh." Now her laughter is joy, and everyone who hears "will laugh" (yitschaq) with her.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Genesis 18:14. Luke 1:37 has ouk adynatesei para tou theou pan rhema, literally no word will be impossible (TAGNT, TBESG). Bengel and the Cambridge Bible on Luke 1:37 point back to Genesis 18:14.
layers.text: The LORD answered Sarah's laugh: "Is anything too difficult for the LORD?" The Greek Old Testament asks whether any word is impossible with God. Pointing Mary to barren Elizabeth, Gabriel answers in nearly the same Greek: "no word from God will ever fail."

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible, Ellicott and the NET Bible notes on Genesis 21:9: the same verb as laugh, in an intensive form. The Cambridge Bible says Paul follows a rabbinic reading of the word as teasing and persecution.
layers.text: Even the trouble that follows uses the name's verb: Ishmael's "mocking" is tsachaq, "laugh," in a stronger form. One old Jewish reading took it as teasing and persecution, and Paul follows it: "the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit."

layers.evidence: Barnes on Romans 4:19 compares Abraham's age in Genesis 17:17.
layers.text: The New Testament makes this birth the model of faith. Abraham was "fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised," and Sarah "considered Him faithful who had promised." Believers, "like Isaac, are children of promise."

layers.evidence: Targum Onkelos on Genesis 17:17 has vachadi, and he rejoiced (Aramaic, Sefaria). Gill ties John 8:56 to the laughter and to Isaac's name; Westcott and others point to Isaac's birth (Pulpit Commentary); Meyer rejects the link to the laughter.
layers.text: Jesus said, "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad." An Aramaic paraphrase turns Abraham's laugh (17:17) into joy. Some tie Jesus' words to that laughter; others point to Isaac's birth or reject the laughter link.

passages.saying: God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God tests Abraham by asking for Isaac, then stops his hand and provides a ram to offer in Isaac's place.

"Provide" is the Hebrew verb ra'ah, "to see." Abraham names the place "The LORD Will Provide" (literally "will see"), and the saying grows: "On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided," or more literally, it will be seen. God sees the need and meets it.

Moriah is named in only one other verse: Solomon builds the temple "on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared" (the same verb, ra'ah). Most readers take it as the same place, so the mountain of the substitute ram becomes the place of Israel's sacrifices.
Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and that "in a sense" (literally "in a parable") he received Isaac back from death.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) notes that the Greek Old Testament often renders yachid with this word
layers.text: "You have not withheld your only son" returns in Paul's "He who did not spare His own Son" (Romans 8:32). The Greek Old Testament calls Isaac Abraham's "beloved" son, a word it often uses for yachid, "only," and many hear Isaac in the Father's "You are My beloved Son" (Mark 1:11).

Isaac carries the wood up the hill as Jesus carries His cross, and "God Himself will provide the lamb" is answered by "Look, the Lamb of God." These are old Christian readings; the New Testament does not draw them itself.

passages.saying: And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God’s angels were going up and down the ladder.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, BDB, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Genesis Rabbah, classic commentaries, a Ligonier devotional by Derek Thomas and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Fleeing the brother he cheated, Jacob sleeps in the open with a stone under his head and dreams of a ladder, or stairway, joining earth and heaven. The LORD renews Abraham's promise: "Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go."

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH.
layers.text: Jacob wakes afraid: "This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!" So he names the place Bethel, "house of God," though until then the town had been called Luz.

layers.evidence: Literal wording of Genesis 11:4 from the STEPBible TAHOT word glosses. Babylon as gate of God from the NET Bible note on 11:9. The contrast of Babel and Bethel is Derek Thomas's (Snakes and Ladders, Ligonier).
layers.text: Babel's tower was to have, literally, its top in the heavens; Jacob's stairway has "its top reaching up to heaven," the same Hebrew words. Babylon's name meant "gate of God"; Bethel is "the gate of heaven." At Babel people reach up; at Bethel God reaches down.

layers.evidence: Genesis Rabbah 68:12 (Sefaria), paraphrased.
layers.text: The last word, bo, can mean "on it" or "on him." An ancient Jewish commentary records two rabbis disagreeing: the angels went up and down the ladder, or on Jacob. When Jesus retells the dream, a person stands where the ladder was: "on the Son of Man."

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 1:51 calls Christ the real ladder, and the Expositor's Greek Testament says He turns earth into a Bethel. OpenBible.info cross-references link the verses.
layers.text: Jesus tells Nathanael, "you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man," in the dream's own order: up first, then down. Jesus Himself is now the stairway between heaven and earth.

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH. Dolos in the Septuagint of Genesis 27:35. Ellicott on John 1:47 hears the contrast: Nathanael lives up to the name Israel and has none of Jacob's guile.
layers.text: Jacob means "heel holder" or "supplanter"; Esau says, "he has cheated me twice." Isaac's "came deceitfully" is dolos in the Greek Old Testament, and Jesus calls Nathanael "a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit": no dolos, nothing of the old Jacob.

layers.evidence: Under Strong's numbering, Genesis 32:28 and Hosea 12:3 are the verb's only two uses (STEPBible TAHOT). BDB reads the next line, Hosea 12:4, he struggled with the angel, as the same verb.
layers.text: Hosea retells Jacob's life: "In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God," and "he found Him at Bethel." "Wrestled" is sarah, the verb inside the name Israel (32:28). The heel-grabber who met God at Bethel became Israel.

passages.saying: This time I will praise the LORD.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, BDB, the NET Bible notes and classic older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Laban tricked Jacob into marrying Leah, and Jacob "loved Rachel more than Leah." But "When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb." She bore four sons in a row, and each name came out of her pain and her hope.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from the NET Bible notes and TBESH. The NET notes call Leah's explanation of Reuben a popular etymology, not an exact one, and say the meaning of Levi is debated.
layers.text: Each name echoes her words. Reuben, "look, a son": "The LORD has seen my affliction." Simeon, "heard": "the LORD has heard that I am unloved." Levi sounds like lavah, "to join": "my husband will become attached to me." Some are puns, not exact meanings.

layers.evidence: Both verses have happa'am (STEPBible TAHOT). The NET Bible notes gloss Judah as he will be praised; Keil and Delitzsch, as the one for whom the LORD is praised; BDB, probably praised.
layers.text: Her third and fourth sayings share a Hebrew word, happa'am, "this time" (in 29:34 the BSB has "Now at last"). The third hopes Jacob will be joined to her. The fourth does not mention him: "This time I will praise the LORD." Judah means "praised."

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on Numbers 18:2 calls yillavu a wordplay with Levi and links it to Leah's hope in Genesis 29:34.
layers.text: The pun on Levi returns when God gives the Levites their work: they are to "join you and assist you" (join is yillavu). Leah hoped her husband would be joined to her; her son's tribe is joined to the priests to serve at God's tent.

layers.evidence: TBESG derives Ioudaios from Ioudas, Judah. Bengel and Gill on Romans 2:29 hear an allusion to Judah's name; Vincent's Word Studies says possibly, comparing Genesis 49:8.
layers.text: The word "Jew" (Ioudaios) comes from Judah. So when Paul says a true Jew is one inwardly, whose "praise does not come from men, but from God," some commentators hear a play on Judah, "praise," though one calls it only a possibility.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Genesis 29:35: the wife who came first but was not preferred is the mother of the seed.
layers.text: God's answer to the unloved wife went far beyond what she asked. Through Levi she became the mother of Israel's priests, and through Judah of its kings. Matthew's genealogy of "Jesus, who is called Christ" runs through "Judah and his brothers."

passages.saying: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, BDB, the NET Bible notes, classic commentaries, Richard Steiner's JBL article, the Dead Sea Scroll 4Q252, Targum Onkelos, the Talmud, Justin Martyr and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: On his deathbed Jacob blesses his sons. Judah, the fourth, receives the royal line: "your father’s sons shall bow down to you," and the ruler's staff will stay with his tribe until a coming one receives the obedience of the nations.

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH. Keil and Delitzsch and the Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 49:8 note the play on yadah, to praise.
layers.text: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you" plays on his name, which means "praised." At his birth Leah said, "This time I will praise the LORD," and named him Judah. The verb is yadah both times.
The near fulfillment came with David, of the tribe of Judah: "Judah prevailed over his brothers and a ruler came from him," and God promised David, "your throne will be established forever."

layers.evidence: TBESH: the meaning is uncertain. BDB calls shello, he whose it is, the best reading, though not certain; the NET Bible's rendering follows the ancient versions. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch see the Messiah in Ezekiel 21:27; Richard Steiner (JBL 132, 2013) sees Nebuchadnezzar.
layers.text: No one is sure what "Shiloh" means. A favored reading, though not certain, is shello, "whose it is." Ezekiel seems to echo it: "until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs." Older commentators see the Messiah there; one recent scholar sees Nebuchadnezzar.

layers.evidence: Dead Sea Scroll 4Q252 5:3 (Intertextual Bible translation; dated there to 160 to 60 BC). Targum Onkelos on Genesis 49:10 has meshicha, Messiah, whose is the kingdom (Aramaic, Sefaria). Talmud, Sanhedrin 98b, paraphrased.
layers.text: Jewish readers heard the Messiah here too. A Dead Sea Scroll from before Jesus' birth reads it as the coming of the righteous Messiah, the branch of David. An Aramaic paraphrase names the Messiah outright, and in the Talmud one school says Shiloh is his name.

layers.evidence: Commentaries on Revelation 5:5 (Bible Hub) and OpenBible.info cross-references link it to Genesis 49:9.
layers.text: Revelation takes up Jacob's lion: "Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed." Then John sees "a Lamb who appeared to have been slain." The King from Judah wins by being slain; as Hebrews says, "our Lord descended from Judah."

layers.evidence: Hebrew ayir (colt) and aton (donkey) in both verses (STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH). Richard Steiner (JBL 132, 2013) notes that scholars have often linked the verses. Justin Martyr, First Apology 32, about AD 155.
layers.text: "He ties his donkey to the vine, his colt to the choicest branch." Zechariah's king rides "on a colt, the foal of a donkey," the same two Hebrew words. Matthew finds "a donkey tied there, with her colt"; an early Christian writer saw Jacob's colt in it.

passages.saying: As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, the NET Bible notes, Genesis Rabbah, classic older commentaries named under each note and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: After Jacob dies, Joseph's brothers fear he will finally pay them back for selling him into slavery. Joseph weeps and tells them not to be afraid: their evil plan had been God's plan to keep many people alive.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Genesis 50:20 notes that the same verb is used for both, contrasting the two purposes. Chashav from TBESH.
layers.text: "You intended" and "God intended" are one Hebrew verb, chashav, to plan. The repetition sets human purpose against God's: one event had two authors with opposite aims, and God's aim stood.

Joseph had said it when he first revealed himself: "it was to save lives that God sent me before you," and "it was not you who sent me here, but God." The psalm tells it from heaven's side: "He sent a man before them," "Joseph, sold as a slave."

layers.evidence: Genesis Rabbah 85:11 (Sefaria) hears God repaying Judah in his own words. In 42:7 treated them as strangers is the same verb, nakar, again. Word data from STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH.
layers.text: "Examine it," the brothers tell Jacob, showing him the bloody robe. "Please examine them," Tamar tells Judah, sending his seal and staff. Both are haker-na, and each man "recognized" (nakar). Later Joseph "recognized them," but "they did not recognize him."

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on Genesis 37:31 points out that Jacob had deceived his own father with two young goats.
layers.text: The deceiver is deceived the same way. Jacob once fooled his blind father with goat skins; now his sons fool him with Joseph's robe dipped in a goat's blood.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Acts 7:9 sees the same envy leading their descendants to hand over Jesus.
layers.text: Stephen tells Joseph's story as a pattern: "Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him." He ends with "the Righteous One" whom his hearers betrayed, as their fathers had betrayed Joseph.

layers.evidence: Gill on Genesis 50:20 draws the comparison with the cross.
layers.text: The cross has the same shape. Peter says Jesus "was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death." Human evil and God's saving purpose meet in one event, though Acts does not mention Joseph.

passages.saying: She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.”
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, BDB, the NET Bible notes and classic older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew baby boy thrown "into the Nile." One mother set her son in a basket "among the reeds along the bank of the Nile," and Pharaoh's own daughter found him, "had compassion on him," and raised him: "he became her son."

layers.evidence: Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible and the NET Bible notes on Exodus 2:10: most agree the name is Egyptian, from a word meaning born or son. I drew him is meshitihu, from mashah (STEPBible TAHOT). The Cambridge Bible says the explanation rests on likeness of sound, not on etymology.
layers.text: Moses (Mosheh) is most likely an Egyptian name, from a word meaning "born" or "son." In Hebrew it sounds like mashah, "to draw out," and the princess makes it a Hebrew pun: "I drew him out of the water." It is a play on sound, not the name's origin.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible notes on Exodus 2:10 read Mosheh as an active form, the one who draws out, and cite Isaiah 63:11; the Cambridge Bible says drawn out would be a different Hebrew form. The TBESH gloss, drawn, gives the sense of the pun, not the form. Keil and Delitzsch, quoting Kurtz, call the name an unintended prophecy.
layers.text: The Hebrew form is active: Mosheh means one who draws out, not one drawn out. The name became an unintended prophecy: the baby drawn from the Nile led Israel through the sea. Isaiah remembers "the days of Moses" and "He who brought them through the sea."

layers.evidence: Mashah occurs only in Exodus 2:10, 2 Samuel 22:17 and Psalm 18:16 (STEPBible TAHOT, BDB). The Cambridge Bible on Psalm 18:16 says there may be an allusion to Exodus 2:10; Gill offers it as one of two readings, the other a drowning man.
layers.text: Mashah, "draw out," occurs only three times: here, and twice in David's song of rescue: "He drew me out of deep waters." Each time the verb comes with water. Some commentators think David may be recalling Moses, or simply picturing a drowning man.

layers.evidence: The Expositor's Greek Testament, Meyer, Bengel, the Cambridge Bible and Ellicott on Acts 7:35 see Stephen setting Moses beside Jesus as a type of Christ.
layers.text: Stephen retells this life as a pattern. The man Israel rejected with "Who made you ruler and judge over us?" is "the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer." Commentators see Stephen setting Moses beside Jesus, whom his hearers had also rejected.

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible on Hebrews 11:24: Scripture mentions the matter only in Exodus 2:10 and Acts 7:22-25.
layers.text: Hebrews recalls the adoption: "By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter." The prince drawn from the river "chose to suffer oppression with God’s people" and "valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt."

passages.saying: I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, BDB, Strong's, the Septuagint, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: At the burning bush Moses asks what to tell Israel when they ask God's name. God answers, "I AM WHO I AM," then calls Himself the LORD, the God of their fathers, and says, "This is My name forever."

layers.evidence: TAHOT tags ehyeh as hayah, to be. BDB lists several derivations of YHWH but says most take it from this verb; Strong's: the self-existent or eternal One. The gloss the existing One is TBESH's
layers.text: The answer plays on the name. "I AM" is ehyeh, from hayah, "to be." The next verse gives the name YHWH, "the LORD," which most scholars derive from the same verb, with a sense like "the existing One."

layers.evidence: Pulpit, Barnes and Gill on John 8:58 point to Exodus 3:14. The Septuagint of Exodus 3:14 reads ego eimi ho on, I am the One who is; in Isaiah 43:10 it has ego eimi where the BSB has I am He
layers.text: Jesus says, "before Abraham was born, I am!" and His hearers "picked up stones to throw at Him." Many commentators hear the name from the bush: in the Greek Old Testament God's answer begins ego eimi, "I am," and Isaiah's "I am He" is ego eimi too.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Revelation 1:4: a paraphrase of the name revealed to Moses, kept in the nominative as if it could not be declined; Ellicott calls the break in grammar intentional. TAGNT: the critical texts read apo ho on
layers.text: Revelation greets the churches "from Him who is and was and is to come," which one commentary calls a paraphrase of the name given to Moses. John even breaks Greek grammar, leaving "Him who is" (ho on) unchanged after "from," as if the Name could not change.

Jesus finds the resurrection in this same scene. At the bush God called Himself "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob," long after they had died, and Jesus concludes: "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 18:6 hears the name I AM in the answer; Barnes finds no proof of miraculous power; the Cambridge Bible leaves open natural awe or a supernatural effect
layers.text: When soldiers come for "Jesus of Nazareth," He answers "I am He" (ego eimi), and "they drew back and fell to the ground." Some commentators hear the divine name again; others think the men were simply overawed.

passages.saying: Israel is My firstborn son
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG (Abbott-Smith), the Septuagint, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: God sends Moses to tell Pharaoh, "Israel is My firstborn son," and to let God's son go. Pharaoh refuses, and at the last plague the LORD "struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt."

layers.evidence: Pulpit on Matthew 2:15: Hosea's words rest on Exodus 4:22. Ellicott: they refer to the history of Israel. Cambridge Bible: Israel's history is treated as typical of the Messiah's life
layers.text: Hosea looks back on the exodus: "out of Egypt I called My son." Matthew sets this beside the child Jesus' stay in Egypt and calls it "fulfilled." It first meant Israel's past; commentators see Matthew reading Israel's story as a pattern for the Messiah's.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Exodus 4:19 and Matthew 2:20 (TAGNT) share the words tethnekasin gar, hoi zetountes and ten psychen. Ellicott, JFB and Meyer on Matthew 2:20 take the parallel as deliberate
layers.text: The angel tells Joseph to go home, "for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead," the words God spoke to Moses in Midian: "all the men who sought to kill you are dead." In the Greek Old Testament the two sentences are almost word for word the same.

layers.evidence: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:16 and 6:13. Cambridge Bible on Matthew 4: the forty years were to Israel what the forty days are to Jesus, and His test of sonship is obedience and trust in God
layers.text: Israel, God's son, was tested forty years in the wilderness, disciplined "just as a man disciplines his son." Tested forty days, Jesus hears "If You are the Son of God," and answers three times from Deuteronomy. Where the first son failed, this Son stands.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (in TBESG): exodos, a going out, used of death in Luke 9:31 and 2 Peter 1:15. Barnes: perhaps an allusion to Israel's departure from Egypt; Gill: the name of the second book of Moses; Cambridge Bible: a very unusual word for death
layers.text: On the mountain Moses and Elijah talk with Jesus about "His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem." The Greek word is exodos, as in "the exodus of the Israelites." It can just mean death, but with Moses there, many hear a new exodus.

layers.evidence: Exodus 13:2 and 13:15. Meyer calls Luke's line a very free quotation of Exodus 13:2; Gill and JFB tie the law to the sparing of Israel's firstborn in Egypt
layers.text: Because God spared Israel's firstborn when Egypt's died, every firstborn son belonged to the LORD and had to be redeemed. Luke quotes this law when Mary's firstborn is presented at the temple: "Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord."

passages.saying: when I see the blood, I will pass over you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: On the night of the last plague each household kills a lamb and puts its blood on the doorframe, and the LORD passes over the marked houses.
The feast is named for the act: pesach (Passover) comes from pasach, "to pass over." The text explains the name itself: "It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses."
Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed," and Peter calls Him "a lamb without blemish or spot," like the unblemished lamb the law required.

When the soldiers do not break Jesus' legs, John says Scripture was fulfilled: "Not one of His bones will be broken." The words fit the Passover rule and also Psalm 34:20; scholars discuss which John means, and many think both.

In John, Jesus is sentenced on "the day of Preparation for the Passover," when the lambs were slaughtered, and at the cross a sponge is lifted to Him on hyssop, the plant used to put the blood on the doorframes.

The lamb runs from Egypt to the end of the Bible: "Look, the Lamb of God" and the Lamb at the center of the throne "who appeared to have been slain." These draw on the Passover lamb and on Isaiah's servant "led like a lamb to the slaughter."

passages.saying: See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG (Abbott-Smith), BDB, Thayer, the Septuagint, the Mishnah, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: God tells Moses to build a sanctuary "so that I may dwell among them," and to make it "according to the pattern I show you." The tent and its furniture follow a pattern Moses was shown on the mountain.

Hebrews quotes this verse and draws the conclusion: the earthly sanctuary "is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven." So Christ "did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself."

layers.evidence: TBESH: tavnit, pattern, plan, form. Abbott-Smith (in TBESG) lists typos for tavnit in the Septuagint of Exodus 25:40 (in 25:9 the Septuagint has paradeigma). TAGNT: typos in Hebrews 8:5 and Romans 5:14
layers.text: "Pattern" is tavnit, a plan or form. The Greek Old Testament renders it typos here, and Hebrews keeps that word when it quotes the verse. Paul uses the same typos when he calls Adam "a pattern of the One to come."

layers.evidence: BDB: kapporet from kipper, cover over sin; the Septuagint has hilasterion, as does Hebrews 9:5 (Abbott-Smith, in TBESG). Thayer gives both readings for Romans 3:25, the mercy seat or an atoning sacrifice, and notes scholars who reject the first
layers.text: The ark's lid, the "mercy seat," is kapporet, from kipper, "to atone," and was sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement. In Greek it is hilasterion, Paul's word for Christ: God "presented Him as the atoning sacrifice." Whether he means the lid is debated.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (in TBESG): katapetasma is chiefly the veil of the Most Holy Place in the Septuagint, and His flesh in Hebrews 10:20. JFB on Hebrews 10:20: the temple veil, a type of His flesh, was torn as He died
layers.text: Behind the veil only the high priest could go, "once a year, and never without blood." When Jesus died, "the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom," and Hebrews speaks of "the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body."

Hebrews says the floor plan itself carried a message: "the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing." Christ "entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood."

layers.evidence: Mishnah Yoma 5:1, paraphrased. Vaughan, quoted in the Expositor's Greek Testament on Hebrews 9:28, sees the high priest coming back out to the anxiously waiting people
layers.text: On the Day of Atonement the people waited for the high priest to come out; by Jewish tradition he kept his prayer short so as not to alarm them. One commentator hears this in Hebrews: Christ "will appear a second time" to "those who eagerly await Him."

passages.saying: The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, BDB, Strong's, the Mishnah and Talmud, the Epistle of Barnabas, Justin Martyr, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: On the Day of Atonement two goats make one sin offering. One is sacrificed; over the other the high priest confesses "all the iniquities" of Israel, puts them on its head, and sends it away alive into the wilderness.

layers.evidence: The Hebrew is la-azazel. TBESH: Azazel, meaning uncertain. Strong's: goat of departure, which Tyndale (1530) rendered scapegoat. BDB: entire removal, and most take it as the name of a spirit haunting the desert. The solitary place (gezerah) is a land cut off: Cambridge Bible, Barnes, Keil and Delitzsch; TBESH: a separation
layers.text: The goat is "for Azazel," a word of uncertain meaning. It has been read as "goat of departure," which gave English "scapegoat," or "entire removal"; most scholars take it as a desert spirit's name. In any case, it goes to a land "cut off," with no way back.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: nasa (H5375) and avonot (H5771) in Leviticus 16:22, avonot in Isaiah 53:11, nasa in 53:12. Ellicott and JFB on Hebrews 9:28: taken from Isaiah 53:12. Pulpit and Gill on Leviticus 16:22 link the goat with Isaiah 53
layers.text: The goat "will carry" (nasa) Israel's "iniquities" (avonot). Isaiah's suffering Servant "will bear their iniquities" (avonot) and "bore the sin of many" (nasa). Hebrews applies that last line to Jesus: "Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many."

layers.evidence: Pulpit and Vincent on Hebrews 13:11: the allusion is to the sin offerings of the Day of Atonement
layers.text: On that day the bodies of the sin offerings whose blood went into the Most Holy Place were burned "outside the camp." Hebrews draws the line to the cross: "Jesus also suffered outside the city gate," so "let us go to Him outside the camp."

layers.evidence: Rabbi Yishmael in Mishnah Yoma 6:8; Talmud Yoma 39b. Both paraphrased
layers.text: An early rabbi taught that a crimson strip turned white when the goat reached the wilderness, citing "Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow." Later tradition says it stopped turning white in the forty years before the temple fell.

layers.evidence: Epistle of Barnabas 7; Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 40
layers.text: Early Christian writers saw Christ in both goats. One reads the cursed goat, sent away with scarlet wool on its head, as a picture of Jesus; another says the two goats point to Christ's two appearances. Leviticus does not say this itself.

passages.saying: you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG (Abbott-Smith), the Septuagint, the Mishnah and Talmud, Philo, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: When harvest began, the first sheaf was waved before the LORD "on the day after the Sabbath." From that day Israel counted seven weeks, "fifty days," to the Feast of Weeks.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Leviticus 23:10: aparche (G536); Abbott-Smith (in TBESG) cites it of Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:20 and 23. Ellicott and Pulpit on 1 Corinthians 15:20: the firstfruits stood for the whole harvest
layers.text: Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep": "Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him." His word, aparche, is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for this sheaf, the pledge of the whole harvest.

layers.evidence: JFB and Bengel on 1 Corinthians 15:20; Meyer leaves it undecided. Mishnah Menachot 10:3 records the dispute over the date with the Boethusians
layers.text: The sheaf was waved "on the day after the Sabbath," and Jesus' tomb was found empty "very early on the first day of the week," the day after the Passover Sabbath. Some commentators note the match, though Jewish groups disputed which Sabbath Leviticus meant.

layers.evidence: TBESG (Abbott-Smith): pentekostos, fiftieth, the fiftieth day after Passover. TAHOT: chamishim, fifty, in Leviticus 23:16. Barnes, Vincent and Meyer on Acts 2:1 call it a harvest feast
layers.text: Pentecost is Greek for "fiftieth": the Feast of Weeks at the end of the fifty-day count, the feast of "the firstfruits of the wheat harvest." On that day the Spirit came, and "about three thousand were added to the believers."

layers.evidence: Talmud Pesachim 68b (Rabbi Elazar), paraphrased. Barnes on Acts 2:1: later Jews kept Pentecost for the giving of the law, but there is no trace of this in the Old Testament
layers.text: Israel reached Sinai "in the third month," the season of this feast, and later Jewish tradition remembered it as the day the law was given, though the Old Testament itself never says so. The law came at Sinai; the Spirit came at Pentecost.

layers.evidence: Philo, On the Decalogue 46 (Yonge translation), paraphrased. Barnes and Ellicott on Acts 2:3 tie Pentecost to the fire at Sinai
layers.text: Sinai came with fire and a ram's-horn blast; Pentecost brings "tongues like flames of fire," and each hears "his own language." A Jewish writer of Jesus' own day pictured the voice at Sinai as a flame that spoke in a language its hearers knew.

passages.saying: proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants. It shall be your Jubilee
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG (Abbott-Smith), the Dead Sea Scroll 11QMelchizedek, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Every fiftieth year Israel was to "proclaim liberty in the land": land went back to the family that held it, and Israelites who had sold themselves were "released in the Year of Jubilee." The land was God's: "it is Mine."

layers.evidence: TBESH: yovel, ram's horn, and the jubilee year marked by its blowing. Keil and Delitzsch on Leviticus 25:9: liberty could begin only with the full forgiveness of sins
layers.text: Jubilee is yovel, "ram's horn": the year is named for the horn that announced it. The horn sounded "on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement," so liberty began on the day Israel's sins were atoned for.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qara (H7121) with deror (H1865) in both Leviticus 25:10 and Isaiah 61:1. JFB and Ellicott on Luke 4:19 see the Jubilee here
layers.text: Isaiah's anointed one is sent "to proclaim liberty to the captives" and "the year of the LORD’s favor." "Proclaim liberty" is the Jubilee's own phrase, qara deror. The prophet takes the Jubilee as a picture of the great release God will bring.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible on Luke 4:19: the primary reference is to the year of Jubilee, which the Cambridge Bible takes as a type of Christ's kingdom
layers.text: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads this passage, rolls up the scroll, and says, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing." Commentators hear the Jubilee in "the year of the Lord’s favor": Jesus announces Himself as its fulfillment.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (in TBESG): aphesis stands for yovel and deror in the Septuagint; release in Luke 4:18, and pardon of sins. TAGNT: 17 uses in the New Testament, two in Luke 4:18 and 15 of sins, as in Luke 24:47
layers.text: Luke's word for "liberty" is aphesis, which the Greek Old Testament uses for the Jubilee and its liberty. In the New Testament it usually means "forgiveness," as in "repentance and forgiveness of sins." Release and forgiveness are one word.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Luke 4:20; JFB on Luke 4:19
layers.text: Jesus rolls up the scroll mid-sentence, after "the year of the Lord’s favor," before Isaiah's "and the day of our God’s vengeance." One commentator says He let grace have the last word; another, that vengeance was only for those who rejected His message.

layers.evidence: 11QMelchizedek, mid-first century BC, cites Leviticus 25:13 and Isaiah 61:1 and names Melchizedek as the heavenly deliverer (Posen Library)
layers.text: A Dead Sea Scroll from before Jesus already read Leviticus 25 and Isaiah 61 together about the last days: a heavenly deliverer brings release to the captives on a Day of Atonement at the end of the tenth jubilee.

passages.saying: Moses gave to Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG (Abbott-Smith), BDB, Strong's, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Justin Martyr, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Joshua son of Nun was Moses' "young assistant." Moses gave him his new name (Numbers records it with the spies, though Exodus already calls him Joshua), and after Moses died God told him to "cross over the Jordan into the land."

layers.evidence: TBESH: Hoshea, salvation; Joshua, Jehovah is salvation. Strong's: from the LORD's name and yasha, to save. BDB also lists the meaning Yah is opulence
layers.text: Hoshea means "salvation." Moses adds Yeho-, a short form of God's name, and makes Yehoshua, which means that the LORD is salvation. The new name says who saves.

layers.evidence: TBESG (Abbott-Smith): Iesous is Jesus in Matthew 1:21 and Joshua in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8. NET Bible note on Matthew 1:21: the name is the Hebrew Yeshua (Joshua), meaning Yahweh saves
layers.text: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are one name, Iesous; the BSB writes "Joshua" for it in Acts 7:45. So the angel's words rest on its Hebrew meaning, "Yahweh saves": "you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins."

layers.evidence: Gill on Hebrews 4:8: Hoshea, Joshua and Jesus are one and the same name; Barnes: Jesus is the Greek way of writing Joshua. The Cambridge Bible calls Joshua's rest a dim shadow of the final rest Christ offers
layers.text: Joshua led Israel in, and "the LORD gave them rest on every side." Yet Hebrews says that if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day: "There remains, then, a Sabbath rest." Commentators call Joshua's rest a shadow of Christ's.

layers.evidence: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 113 (second century)
layers.text: Moses saw the land but heard, "you will not cross into it"; Joshua led the people over. An early Christian writer saw Christ here: Joshua, not Moses, brought the people in, as Jesus will gather His scattered people. The New Testament does not say this.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Zechariah 6:11: Iesous. NET Bible note on Zechariah 6:12: Branch (tsemach) comes from the verb for branch out; Zerubbabel in the immediate context, Jesus as the ultimate referent. TBESH: mofet, sign, a token of something to come. Justin Martyr, Dialogue 115, reads Zechariah 3 of Christ
layers.text: After the exile the high priest Joshua is crowned and told, "Here is a man whose name is the Branch." He and his companions are "a sign" of "My servant, the Branch," and in Greek his name is Iesous. Some see in the Branch first Zerubbabel, then Jesus.

passages.saying: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, the Dead Sea Scroll 4QTestimonia, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: At Horeb the people begged not to hear God's voice or "see this great fire anymore." God answers with a promise: He will raise up a prophet like Moses and "put My words in his mouth."

layers.evidence: Deuteronomy 18:20-22. The Cambridge Bible reads a prophet as the succession of prophets; Keil and Delitzsch agree but include Christ as its culmination; Barnes sees a line of prophets ending in one eminent individual
layers.text: The near fulfillment is the line of prophets after Moses: the chapter goes straight on to tests for true and false prophets. Some commentators stop there; others see that line reaching its height in Christ, one great Prophet.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: yaqim (18:15) and qam (34:10) are both qum. Benson and Gill read the verse as still awaiting the prophet; Jewish tradition (Sifre 357) reads it as Moses' unmatched past
layers.text: Yet Deuteronomy closes by saying no such prophet had arisen: "Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses." "Risen" is the same verb, qum, as "raise up." Some Christian commentators read this as Israel still waiting for the prophet like Moses.

layers.evidence: 4QTestimonia, mid-first century BC, quotes Deuteronomy 18:18-19 beside Numbers 24:15-17 (a king) and Deuteronomy 33:8-11 (a priest). Gill on Deuteronomy 18:15 cites John 6:14 for the expectation
layers.text: By Jesus' day people expected "the Prophet." John the Baptist is asked, "Are you the Prophet?" and after the loaves the crowd says, "Truly this is the Prophet." A Dead Sea Scroll had already set this promise beside texts about a coming king and priest.

Peter quotes the promise at the temple and applies it to Jesus, with Moses' warning about anyone who will not listen (Acts 3:22-23). Stephen quotes it again before the council: "God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers."

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Mark 9:7; Meyer and Benson on Matthew 17:5
layers.text: At the transfiguration, with Moses standing beside Jesus, the voice from the cloud says, "This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!" Many commentators hear Deuteronomy's "You must listen to him" in those words.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 1:18: the primary reference is still to Moses; the Cambridge Bible glosses it as not even Moses
layers.text: Moses was set apart because the LORD spoke with him "face to face." John says the Son goes further: "No one has ever seen God," but the Son "has made Him known," and "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ."

passages.saying: anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, the Septuagint, the Mishnah, Josephus, the Temple Scroll (as translated by Torleif Elgvin), Justin Martyr, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: If an executed criminal's body was hung on a tree, it had to come down and be buried the same day, "because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse." Joshua kept the rule, having the bodies of five kings taken down "at sunset."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qillat (H7045) Elohim taluy (H8518). The Septuagint has cursed by God (hypo theou). Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4, paraphrased
layers.text: The Hebrew, qillat Elohim taluy, reads word for word "curse of God," "hanged one." It can mean cursed by God, as the Greek Old Testament took it, or an offense against God: early Jewish law says leaving the body up would desecrate God's name.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible and Vincent on Galatians 3:13 note that Paul omits by God (hypo theou), which the Septuagint has; TAGNT confirms Galatians 3:13 has no hypo theou
layers.text: Paul quotes this verse to explain the cross: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." His wording, "Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree," leaves God's name out. The curse He bore opens Abraham's blessing to the Gentiles.

layers.evidence: Acts 5:30 and 10:39. Ellicott on Acts 5:30: the phrase comes from the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 21; TAGNT: kremasantes epi xylou
layers.text: The apostles described the crucifixion in this law's words, "by hanging Him on a tree," and Peter writes, "He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree." The phrase comes from the Greek Old Testament of this law.

layers.evidence: Josephus, Jewish War 4.5.2 (Whiston translation). Barnes and the Cambridge Bible on John 19:31 cite Deuteronomy 21:23
layers.text: The rule shaped the day Jesus died. The leaders asked that "the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath," and that evening Joseph of Arimathea asked for His body. A Jewish historian of the time says Jews buried even the crucified before sunset.

layers.evidence: The Temple Scroll (11QTemple 64), second century BC, as translated in Torleif Elgvin, The Messiah Who Was Cursed on the Tree, Themelios 22.3
layers.text: Before Jesus, a Dead Sea Scroll already applied this law to men hanged alive, calling those who hang on the tree cursed by God and by men. A crucified Messiah was, as Paul says, "a stumbling block to Jews."

layers.evidence: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 89 (Trypho) and 96 (Justin), ANF translation; Elgvin also cites Trypho's objection
layers.text: In Justin Martyr's second-century Dialogue, Trypho, a Jew, names this verse as his great objection: the law calls anyone crucified accursed. Justin answers that the same verse confirms the hope that rests on the crucified Christ.

passages.saying: you have tied this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, BDB, Strong's, the UBS Handbook on Joshua, 1 Clement, Justin Martyr, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Rahab, a prostitute in Jericho, hides Joshua's two spies and asks them to spare her family. They tell her to tie a scarlet cord in her window and gather everyone inside, and when the city falls, Joshua spares her household.

layers.evidence: TAHOT tags Joshua 2:18 and 2:21 as tiqvah, cord, and 31 other verses, Hosea 2:15 among them, as tiqvah, hope; the rope in 2:15 is chevel. Strong's counts one word, BDB and TBESH two. The UBS Handbook notes the cord sense occurs only here and in 2:21; the hope reading is a ministry site's (ONE FOR ISRAEL, 2018)
layers.text: The cord in the window is not chevel, like her rope, but tiqvah, which means "cord" only here and in 2:21. Over 30 other times it means "hope" ("a gateway of hope"), and some hear that in Rahab's cord. Dictionaries differ on whether it is one word or two.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: both verses end in the heavens above and on the earth below with the same words (mimmaal, mitachat); the openings differ. Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch on Joshua 2:11 cite Deuteronomy 4:39
layers.text: Rahab confesses that "the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below," the confession Moses told Israel to take to heart (Deuteronomy 4:39). In Hebrew the closing phrase is identical. A Canaanite outsider confesses Israel's own creed.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry, Gill and Barnes on Joshua 2:18 compare the scarlet cord with the Passover blood
layers.text: The terms echo the first Passover. Egypt: "None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning." Jericho: "If anyone goes out the door of your house," his blood is on his own head. A sign on the house, the family inside, and judgment passes over.

layers.evidence: 1 Clement 12 (Lightfoot translation); Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 111. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary trace the reading through the early church fathers
layers.text: Early Christian writers saw Christ's blood in the scarlet cord: it showed that redemption would come through the Lord's blood to all who believe and hope in God. The New Testament does not draw this link.

layers.evidence: Pulpit on Matthew 1:5: generally taken as Rahab of Jericho, though the Old Testament is silent on the marriage; Bengel and Meyer agree, and Ellicott notes the silence. Gill: a Gentile in Christ's line. TBESG marks the identification as uncertain
layers.text: Hebrews counts "the prostitute Rahab" among the faithful, and James says she was "justified by her actions." Matthew names a Rahab as Boaz's mother, a Gentile in Jesus' line; most take her to be this one, though the Old Testament records no such marriage.

passages.saying: Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Ruth, a widow from Moab, asks Boaz to marry her and act as her family's kinsman-redeemer. He does, and their son Obed becomes King David's grandfather.

Boaz had prayed that Ruth be rewarded by the LORD, "under whose wings you have taken refuge." Now she asks him to spread his "wing" over her: kanaph means both wing and the corner of a garment. She asks Boaz to become the answer to his own prayer.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from TBESH
layers.text: Naomi means "my delight" and Mara "bitterness." Back in Bethlehem she tells the women, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." The book ends with the LORD giving her a redeemer who "will renew your life."

A kinsman-redeemer (go'el) was the near relative who bought back family land, and a related law had a man marry his dead brother's widow so that "his name will not be blotted out." Boaz does both at once, though exactly how these laws applied is debated.

The prophets use the same words for God. He is Israel's Redeemer (go'el), and in Ezekiel He says, "I spread My cloak over you," with the word kanaph, and "you became Mine." Ruth's request speaks the language of God's covenant love.

Matthew names Boaz and Ruth in Jesus' family line. Many Christians see Boaz, the relative who willingly pays to redeem, as a picture of Christ, "born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law"; the New Testament does not draw the Boaz link itself.

passages.saying: The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, TheTorah.com articles, Enter the Bible, the Talmud, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Hannah, childless and taunted by her rival, prays for a son and then gives him to the LORD's service. Her song of thanks praises a God who reverses fortunes: "He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap."

layers.evidence: Judges 21:25. TAHOT: mashiach occurs earlier only in Leviticus 4:3, 4:5, 4:16 and 6:22, of the priest. The Cambridge Bible and Ellicott on 1 Samuel 2:10 note its first use for a king. Septuagint: the horn of his christos
layers.text: Israel had no king yet, but Hannah ends with "His king" and "His anointed." Mashiach, the word behind Messiah, had so far been used only of "the anointed priest"; this is its first use for a king. The Greek Old Testament has christos.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note on 1 Samuel 1:20: a sound-play, not a strict etymology; the name more probably means name of God. TAHOT: sha'al (H7592) in 1:20, 1:28, 8:10 and 12:17. Pulpit, Cambridge Bible and Keil and Delitzsch on 1:28; Milstein and Aschkenasy (TheTorah.com) on the pun with Saul
layers.text: Hannah explains Samuel's name with a sound-play: "Because I have asked for him from the LORD" (sha'al, to ask). In 1:28 she calls him sha'ul, "asked" (BSB "dedicated"), spelled like the name Saul. Later Israel is "asking him for a king," and gets Saul.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Meyer and the Cambridge Bible on Luke 1:46; Enter the Bible (Luther Seminary) on 1 Samuel 2:1-10
layers.text: Mary's song in Luke 1 is modeled on Hannah's. Hannah: "My heart rejoices in the LORD"; Mary: "my spirit rejoices in God my Savior!" Hannah's God "humbles and He exalts"; Mary's "has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble."

layers.evidence: Enter the Bible (Luther Seminary) and the Reformation Study Bible note the frame. TAHOT: qeren, horn, in 1 Samuel 2:10 and 2 Samuel 22:3; mashiach in 2:10 and 22:51. Barnes on 1 Samuel 2:10 compares Luke 1:69
layers.text: Hannah's song and David's song frame the books of Samuel. Both call God the Rock, sing of a "horn," and end with "His king" and "His anointed." Zechariah takes up the picture for Jesus: God "has raised up a horn of salvation for us" in David's house.

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible and Meyer on Luke 2:52 compare 1 Samuel 2:26
layers.text: Luke describes the boy Jesus in words close to those used of the boy Samuel. Samuel "continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man"; Jesus "grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man."

layers.evidence: Talmud Megillah 14a, paraphrased. Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Samuel 2:10: David's line culminated in the Messiah; the Cambridge Bible: the hymn reaches forward to the King Messiah. TAHOT: qeren in 16:13 and 2:10; pakh, flask, in 10:1
layers.text: Hannah's son anointed Saul from "a flask of oil" but David with "the horn of oil," and Jewish tradition reads her "horn" as a prophecy of David's lasting line. Commentators see that line reaching forward to the Messiah.

passages.saying: He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scroll 4Q174 (Intertextual Bible), F. F. Bruce, New Testament Studies, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: King David, settled in a palace of cedar, wants to build a temple for the ark of God. Through the prophet Nathan, God turns the offer around: David's son will build the temple, and God will build David a dynasty and establish its throne forever.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: bayit (H1004) 15 times in 2 Samuel 7. TBESH: house, also household, family. The closing lesson is Keil and Delitzsch's on 7:11; Gill and Benson make the same turn
layers.text: The chapter turns on bayit, "house," used 15 times. David offers God a house, a temple; God answers, "He Himself will establish a house for you," a dynasty. One commentator draws the lesson: God must build a man's house before the man can build God's.

layers.evidence: Solomon adds: I have built the house for the Name of the LORD (1 Kings 8:20). Benson and Gill on 2 Samuel 7:14: the discipline clause fits Solomon, not Christ
layers.text: The first fulfillment is Solomon, who dedicated the temple saying, "Now the LORD has fulfilled the word that He spoke." The promise even allows for his failures: "When he does wrong, I will discipline him."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Chronicles 17:13: the omission comes from reading David's seed as the Messiah; Ellicott: probably not a mere abridgment; Barnes: the writer is not about to record Solomon's sins
layers.text: Chronicles retells the promise without "When he does wrong," and where Samuel has "Your house and kingdom," it reads "My house and My kingdom." Some commentators say Chronicles reads the son as the Messiah; others, that it simply passes over Solomon's sins.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Hebrews 1:5: Solomon was a first and partial fulfillment; the Cambridge Bible: the words applied first to Solomon; Meyer dissents. Cambridge Bible on Luke 1:32 cites 2 Samuel 7:12
layers.text: Hebrews quotes "I will be His Father, and He will be My Son" of Christ, and the angel tells Mary her son will have "the throne of His father David" and "His kingdom will never end!" Commentators see in Solomon only a first, partial fulfillment.

layers.evidence: 4Q174 (4QFlorilegium) on 2 Samuel 7:11-14, read with Amos 9:11 through the shared verb qum (TAHOT; BSB restore), in the Intertextual Bible translation with a note by Reed Carlson. F. F. Bruce (Encyclopaedia Judaica) on the same text
layers.text: The Dead Sea Scrolls show Jews reading this as a promise of a coming king. One scroll applies it to the Branch of David and links "I will raise up" to Amos's "I will restore the fallen tent of David," the same verb in Hebrew. Acts 15:16 quotes Amos.

layers.evidence: Numbers 12:7. D'Angelo, cited in a New Testament Studies short study (1991), argues Hebrews 3 draws on 1 Chronicles 17:14; Grässer disputes it. Septuagint: pistoso auton en oiko mou; pistoo there means establish (Abbott-Smith; Brenton)
layers.text: Hebrews sets Moses, faithful "in all My house," beside the Son: "Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house." Some scholars also hear 1 Chronicles 17:14, where in Greek God establishes David's son in His house with a verb from the root for "faithful."

passages.saying: Then Elijah took the child, brought him down from the upper room into the house, and gave him to his mother.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, the Septuagint, Working Preacher (Lucy Lind Hogan), OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill on 1 Kings 17:22: the first instance of anyone raised from the dead
layers.text: During a famine Elijah stays with a widow in Zarephath. When her son dies, Elijah stretches himself over the boy and prays, and the LORD restores his life: the first raising of the dead in the Bible. His mother says, "Now I know that you are a man of God."

layers.evidence: Both read kai edoken auton te metri autou: the Septuagint of 1 Kings 17:23 and Luke 7:15 in every edition TAGNT records. Lucy Lind Hogan (Working Preacher, 2016) notes the gate and the giving back; Ellicott and JFB on Luke 7:16 recall Elijah
layers.text: Luke tells how Jesus raised a widow's only son at Nain in the words of Elijah's story. Both stories meet a widow at the town gate, and Luke's Greek for "Jesus gave him back to his mother" matches the Greek Old Testament of this verse word for word.

layers.evidence: Lucy Lind Hogan (Working Preacher, 2016): unlike the prophets, Jesus need only touch the bier, and He does not cry out to God
layers.text: The differences matter too. Elijah "stretched himself out over the child three times" and pleaded with the LORD; Jesus only touches the coffin and speaks: "Young man," He said, "I tell you, get up!" The crowd cries, "A great prophet has appeared among us!"

layers.evidence: Ellicott, JFB and the Cambridge Bible on Luke 4:26: a Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon; Ellicott sees in it the future calling of the Gentiles
layers.text: Jesus Himself pointed to this widow at Nazareth: "Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon," a Gentile town. He named Naaman the Syrian too, and the synagogue crowd was so enraged that it tried to throw Him off a cliff.

layers.evidence: Expositor's Greek Testament on Luke 7:16: Shunem is near Nain. JFB, Gill and the Cambridge Bible on Hebrews 11:35 name the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite
layers.text: Elisha later raised a mother's son at Shunem, near Nain, so Luke's story recalls both prophets. Most commentators read Hebrews' "Women received back their dead, raised to life again" as the widow of Zarephath and the woman of Shunem.

layers.evidence: TBESH: Elijah, my God is Jehovah, or Yah is God. Barnes on 1 Kings 17:1: the name expresses the truth his whole life preached. Pulpit on 1 Kings 18:39: the people turned the prophet's name into a war cry
layers.text: Elijah's name, Eli-yahu, means that the LORD is my God. At Carmel the people's verdict puts his name into words: "The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!" The name sums up the truth his whole life preached.

passages.saying: But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, 1 Clement, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:25: Job knows he will be vindicated, and though he will die, his vindicator lives; the picture is of God rising up to do justice.
layers.text: Job has lost his children, wealth and health, and his friends insist the innocent never perish. Wishing his words were "chiseled in stone forever," he declares that his Redeemer lives and will rise up for him in the end, even if Job himself dies.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 1:9 and 2:3: chinnam means gratis, from the verb chanan (to be gracious) or the noun chen (grace). TBESH H2600: freely, for nothing, without cause.
layers.text: The accuser asks, "Does Job fear God for nothing?" Later God says, "you incited Me against him to ruin him without cause." Both are one Hebrew word, chinnam, related to the word for grace. Will Job fear God for nothing while he suffers for nothing?

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 1:6: with the article, the word's meaning gets prominence. TBESH H7854: adversary, one who withstands. Meyer derives Revelation 12:10 from Zechariah 3 and Job 1 and 2; Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible compare them.
layers.text: Here Satan is ha-satan, "the adversary," the "the" stressing what the word means. He questions Job's motives before God. Revelation celebrates the end of that role: "the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down," a scene set beside Job 1 and Zechariah 3.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 16:19: the witness in heaven must be God. Cambridge Bible on Job 9:33: no prophecy of the incarnation, but the human heart's cry to meet and see God as a man. JFB and Matthew Henry read it of Christ.
layers.text: Job's hope grows: "Nor is there a mediator between us," then "my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high." Christians hear the answer in "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Others see only a cry to meet God as a man.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:25: go'el, from ga'al (to redeem, protect, vindicate); here Job thinks of God as his vindicator. NET on Proverbs 23:11: the LORD is probably the protector there. Cambridge Bible: Job here names God his Goel. TBESH H1350.
layers.text: "Redeemer" is go'el, the next of kin who could "redeem what his brother has sold" and was "the avenger of blood." Proverbs probably gives the title to God as defender of orphans: "their Redeemer is strong." Job, too, surely means God Himself.
