layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:25: an adjective here, an epithet of the vindicator. Cambridge Bible: an epithet of God, but meaning later rather than last. TBESH H0314: later, latter, last. JFB and Poole link it with the First and the Last.
layers.text: "In the end" is acharon, "last," perhaps a title: the Redeemer is the Last. Isaiah pairs the same two words for God, "Redeemer" and "I am the last," and the risen Jesus says, "I am the First and the Last." Some read the title as "later," One who comes after.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:26: the phrase can mean without my flesh or in my flesh. Septuagint (Rahlfs) of 19:26: anastēsai, raise up my skin. 1 Clement 24 and 26: Christ the firstfruits, and Job cited for the raising of this flesh. Barnes sees no necessary reference to resurrection.
layers.text: Verse 26 is hard: the Hebrew "from my flesh" can mean with it or without it. The Greek Old Testament has God raise up Job's skin, and an early Christian writer who calls the risen Jesus the firstfruits cites Job for the raising of our flesh.

passages.saying: You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, Jerome, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 2:7: ancient Near Eastern adoption language from covenants of grant, in which a lord rewarded a faithful subject with the status of son and an inheritance.
layers.text: Kings plot "against the LORD and against His Anointed One," but God has installed His King on Zion, calls him Son and promises him the nations. This is royal adoption language, used of David's line: a faithful subject made a son, with an inheritance.

layers.evidence: Expositor's Greek Testament, Meyer and Gill on Acts 4:27: Herod stands for the psalm's kings and Pilate for its rulers. TAHOT and TAGNT: mashiach (H4899), christos (G5547), chriō (G5548).
layers.text: When the apostles are threatened, the church prays this psalm as current events: Herod and Pilate conspired "against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed." The psalm's "Anointed One" is mashiach (Messiah), in Greek christos (Christ).

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Acts 13:33: this use of the psalm is best explained by Romans 1:4. Poole: Christ did not begin to be Son at the resurrection but was then shown to be.
layers.text: Paul hears the king's "today" as resurrection day: God kept His promise "by raising up Jesus." In Romans, Jesus is "declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection," shown to be Son then, not made Son. Hebrews quotes it too.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Luke 3:22: the words recall Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1; one Greek manuscript (D), several Latin ones and some church fathers quote Psalm 2:7 in full, against the weight of the manuscripts. Ellicott and Pulpit on Matthew 3:17.
layers.text: At Jesus' baptism the voice from heaven says, "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased," recalling this psalm and Isaiah's Servant, "in whom My soul delights." In Luke, a few old copies read the psalm's "today I have become Your Father" instead.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 2:9: the Septuagint reads the consonants as ra'ah (shepherd) rather than ra'a' (break); nafats (smash) in the next line favors break. TAGNT: poimainō in Revelation 2:27, 12:5, 19:15 and 7:17.
layers.text: The Hebrew letters of "You will break them with an iron scepter" can also read "you will shepherd," as the Greek Old Testament took it. Revelation quotes it so (BSB "rule"), and the Lamb "will be their shepherd." But "shatter them like pottery" favors "break."

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Psalm 2:12: bar for son, used in Hebrew only in Proverbs 31:2; the Septuagint renders it as laying hold of instruction. NET Bible notes: bar as an adjective, pure. Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 1.19, defends rendering an uncertain word differently in different places.
layers.text: "Kiss the Son" uses bar, Aramaic for son, where verse 7 has the Hebrew ben; elsewhere Hebrew has bar only in Proverbs 31:2. Some read "pure"; the Greek urges taking hold of instruction. Jerome rendered it both ways, as adoring the Son and as worshiping purely.

passages.saying: what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB and its footnotes, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 8:5: these terms allude to mankind's royal status as God's vice-regents.
layers.text: Looking at "the moon and the stars," David marvels that God cares for frail humans at all, yet has crowned them "with glory and honor" and made them rulers over the animals, as in Genesis 1. These are royal words: humans rule on God's behalf.

layers.evidence: TBESH: enosh, man, mortal man; adam, man, human being. Barnes on Hebrews 2:9: we do not see mankind with the dominion the psalm describes.
layers.text: Hebrews quotes this and admits the gap: "Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him. But we see Jesus." In the psalm "son of man" (ben adam) means a human being, like enosh, "mortal man." What God promised humanity is already true of one man.

layers.evidence: BSB footnote on Psalm 8:5: or than God, or than the heavenly beings; see also the Septuagint. NET Bible notes: Hebrews 2:7 follows the Septuagint. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) on brachy ti cites Hebrews 2:7, 9 for both senses. The Cambridge Bible reads time; Ellicott, rank.
layers.text: In "a little lower than the angels" the Hebrew has elohim, "God" or "the heavenly beings"; Hebrews follows the Greek "angels." Its Greek for "a little" can mean slightly or for a short time, so some read Jesus' lowering as brief, others as a matter of rank.

layers.evidence: Expositor's Greek Testament on 1 Corinthians 15:27: as man, Christ is the countertype of Adam. Ellicott: all things are put under man, and in a higher sense under the Son of Man.
layers.text: Paul joins "You have placed everything under his feet" to Christ's reign: "He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death." The rule given to humanity belongs, in a higher sense, to Christ, the new Adam.

layers.evidence: BSB footnote on Psalm 8:2: literally strength; the Septuagint has praise, cited in Matthew 21:16. Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 21:16: words first applied to Jehovah, which Jesus claims as addressed to Himself.
layers.text: When children in the temple shout "Hosanna to the Son of David!" and leaders object, Jesus quotes verse 2: "From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise." The Hebrew has "strength." Praise once offered to God, Jesus accepts for Himself.

passages.saying: For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, BDB, Josephus, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 16:10: the psalmist speaks of himself, confident that God will prevent him from dying.
layers.text: David trusts the LORD as his "chosen portion," so he is sure God will not hand him over to the grave but show him "the path of life," with "eternal pleasures at Your right hand." He is confident God will keep him from death.

At Pentecost Peter quotes the psalm and argues it cannot mean David: "David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day." As a prophet, David foresaw "the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay."

layers.evidence: Josephus, Antiquities 7.15.3 (Whiston): Hyrcanus the high priest opened one room of David's tomb and took out three thousand talents; many years later King Herod opened another.
layers.text: David's tomb was a landmark. Nehemiah marks repairs "opposite the tombs of David," and an ancient historian says a high priest and later King Herod each took treasure from a room of it. Everyone knew where David lay. But "God has raised this Jesus to life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 16:10: shachat, pit, often a title for Sheol. TBESH H7845: Pit, another name of Sheol. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G1312: corruption of the grave; in the Septuagint chiefly for shachat.
layers.text: "Decay" is the Hebrew shachat, "pit," a name for the grave; the Greek Old Testament has diaphthora, "corruption." Both promise rescue from death. Paul draws the contrast: David "saw decay. But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay."

layers.evidence: BDB on H2623: chasid denotes the active practice of chesed. Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible on Acts 13:34: the Greek for mercies is the adjective translated holy in the next verse. Expositor's Greek Testament: the blessings are ratified and assured in the triumph of God's Holy One.
layers.text: Paul links two verses by one Greek word. Isaiah's "loving devotion promised to David" (chesed) is in Greek the "holy" (hosia) blessings; the psalm's "Holy One" is chasid, one who shows chesed, in Greek hosios. The promises are sure in God's risen Holy One.

passages.saying: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: David cries out to a God who seems silent while enemies surround him, then turns to praise: God has listened, and the nations will worship.
On the cross Jesus cries the psalm's first line in Aramaic: "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"
Some bystanders take "Eloi" (my God) as a call for Elijah. The cry they misunderstood was the opening line of a psalm.
The psalm's details return at the cross: mockers shake their heads and say God should deliver Him, and soldiers divide His garments and cast lots, which John says fulfilled Scripture.

The psalm does not end in despair. Its second half praises God among "my brothers," words Hebrews puts in Jesus' mouth, and it ends with all nations turning to the LORD. Many readers think quoting the first line called the whole psalm to mind.

layers.evidence: STEPBible's TAHOT gives the Leningrad Codex reading ka'ari and notes the Judean Desert reading ka'aru
layers.text: The BSB reads "they have pierced my hands and feet." The traditional Hebrew text has ka'ari, "like a lion," while a manuscript found in the Judean Desert reads ka'aru, "they dug." Christians link the verse to the nail wounds, but the wording is a real textual question.

passages.saying: Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Psalm 41:9: the figure is a horse that turns and kicks the one who fed it; the Pulpit Commentary reads it the same way.
layers.text: Sick in bed, David hears his enemies ask, "When will he die and be forgotten?" Worse, a trusted friend who ate at his table has turned against him, like a horse kicking the one who fed it. David asks God to "raise me up."

At the Last Supper Jesus applies the verse to Judas: "The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me." Soon after, "He dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas." The friend who shared the psalmist's bread now sits at Jesus' own table.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on John 13:18: John changes the Greek psalm's common esthiō to trōgō, used of eating Christ's flesh in John 6 and elsewhere in the New Testament only in Matthew 24:38. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G5176: in late everyday Greek, simply to eat.
layers.text: Jesus' word for "shares" (eats) is trōgō, not the Greek psalm's verb. It is the verb of "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life," though also an everyday word. The betrayer ate with "the bread that came down from heaven."

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Psalm 41:9: Ahithophel almost certainly intended; Poole and Barnes agree. Ellicott on Matthew 27:5: apanchō is the Septuagint's word in 2 Samuel 17:23. TAGNT: G0519 occurs only in Matthew 27:5.
layers.text: Many take David's false friend to be Ahithophel, who sided with Absalom and later "hanged himself." Matthew says Judas "went away and hanged himself," with a verb used nowhere else in the New Testament: the Greek Old Testament's word for Ahithophel.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary and Barnes on John 18:1 recall David's flight from Absalom; the Cambridge Bible says John gives no indication of it.
layers.text: Betrayed by Ahithophel, David "crossed the Kidron Valley" and climbed the Mount of Olives weeping. Betrayed by Judas, Jesus "went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley" to the same hill. Some recall David's flight; others note John is silent on it.

layers.evidence: Meyer on John 13:19: by this prediction, what might have become ground of doubt becomes ground for faith.
layers.text: Jesus names the betrayal in advance on purpose: "I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He." What could have shaken their faith becomes a reason for it.

layers.evidence: Bengel on John 13:18 compares aqev in Genesis 3:15. TAHOT tags both words H6119.
layers.text: "Heel" is aqev, the word of the first promise, where the serpent "will strike his heel" but the woman's seed "will crush your head." Some set the two verses side by side, and John notes that when Judas took the morsel, "Satan entered into him."

passages.saying: zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible, introduction to Psalm 69: no psalm except Psalm 22 is so often quoted in the New Testament.
layers.text: David, sinking into "deep waters," cries to God. He suffers "for Your sake": his devotion to God's house has made him "a stranger to my brothers." Yet the psalm ends in praise. Only Psalm 22 is quoted more often in the New Testament.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 2:17: the change from past to future is itself significant. Bengel: His enemies later killed Jesus for this zeal; Meyer disagrees. TAGNT: the future kataphagetai is in all major Greek texts; the Textus Receptus has the past.
layers.text: When Jesus clears the temple, His disciples remember the line "Zeal for Your house will consume Me." The psalm says "has consumed"; John has the future, "will consume." Some hear His death in that change: His zeal would cost Him His life. Others disagree.

Paul quotes the second half to teach patience with weaker believers: "even Christ did not please Himself." The insults aimed at God fell on Christ, so the strong can "bear with the shortcomings of the weak."

layers.evidence: Septuagint (Rahlfs) of Psalm 69:21: cholē and oxos. The Cambridge Bible and Expositor's Greek Testament see John 19:28 fulfilling it; Gill and EGT link Matthew 27:34. Benson and Gill also cite Psalm 22:15.
layers.text: David's enemies "poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst," in Greek cholē and oxos. On the cross Jesus said "I am thirsty" to fulfill Scripture and was given oxos, sour wine; Matthew says He was first offered wine "mixed with gall."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: chinnam (H2600) in Psalm 69:4, Psalm 35:19 and Job 2:3; John 15:25 has dōrean (G1432). NET Bible notes on Job 2:3: chinnam means gratis, without cause.
layers.text: Jesus applies the psalm's "Those who hate me without cause" to His own enemies: "They hated Me without reason." Psalm 35:19 has the same Hebrew. The key word is chinnam, "for nothing," the word God uses of Job's undeserved suffering.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible, introduction to Psalm 69: not prediction but description; each suffering servant of God was in some measure a type of the true Servant, which explains its use as a Proper Psalm for Good Friday.
layers.text: Peter applies verse 25 to Judas, turning "their place" into "his place." One classic reading calls the psalm description, not prediction: each servant who suffered for God's sake in some measure foreshadowed the true Servant. So it became a Good Friday psalm.

passages.saying: Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB and its footnotes, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, the Wisdom of Solomon, Athanasius, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling out "beside the gates to the city." She says she was with God before creation, "I was there when He established the heavens," and promises, "whoever finds me finds life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Proverbs 8:22: two Hebrew roots qanah, to possess and to create (Genesis 14:19; Deuteronomy 32:6). BSB footnote: or possessed. Athanasius, Discourse II Against the Arians 1 and 11.
layers.text: "The LORD created me" uses qanah, which can mean "to possess" or "to create," as when God is "Creator of heaven and earth." Arius read "created" to make the Son a creature; Athanasius said it speaks of the Word becoming man. Both read Wisdom as the Son.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Proverbs 8:30: master craftsman or nursing child; craftsman has the most support (Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac). TBESH: amon, skilled workman; sachaq, to laugh, play.
layers.text: "Skilled craftsman" is amon, a rare word: "master craftsman" or "nursing child." A child fits Wisdom being "brought forth," but craftsman has more support. "Rejoicing" is sachaq, "to laugh, play": Wisdom delights before God and "in the sons of men."

layers.evidence: Septuagint (Rahlfs) of Proverbs 8:23: en archē. The Cambridge Bible, Benson and Gill on John 1:1 point to Proverbs 8.
layers.text: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" recalls Genesis 1 and also Wisdom, at God's side "from the beginning, before the earth began." The Greek of 8:23 even has John's opening words, en archē. But John goes further: "the Word was God."

layers.evidence: TAGNT: apaugasma occurs in the New Testament only at Hebrews 1:3. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G0541: in the Septuagint only at Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, a book not in the Hebrew Bible, where Wisdom is the apaugasma of eternal light and the eikōn of God's goodness. Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible on Hebrews 1:3; Ellicott on Colossians 1:15.
layers.text: Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God’s glory." The Greek Old Testament has that word only in the Wisdom of Solomon, a book outside the Hebrew Bible: Wisdom is the radiance of eternal light and image of God's goodness. Paul calls the Son God's "image."

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Luke 11:49: He identifies Himself with the Wisdom of God; Barnes agrees. The Cambridge Bible also weighs a lost book of that name; Ellicott finds no trace of one.
layers.text: Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God." In Luke, Jesus quotes "the wisdom of God": "I will send them prophets and apostles." In Matthew He says it in His own voice: "I am sending you prophets." Many hear Him speaking as God's Wisdom.

passages.saying: Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), the Mishnah (Joshua Kulp's translation), and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Song 8:6: in the ancient Near East a seal denoted ownership.
layers.text: The bride asks to be worn as a seal on her beloved's heart and arm, and a seal marked ownership. Love like this cannot be put out or bought: "Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away." Earlier she sang, "My beloved is mine and I am his."

layers.evidence: TBESH: shalhevet, flame; Yah, a shortened form of the LORD's name. TAHOT glosses it a flame of the Lord. NET Bible notes: the Masoretes did not point it as the divine name; most likely an intensive. Ellicott: the only sacred name in the book, used as a superlative. Cambridge Bible: a flame kindled and cherished by God.
layers.text: "The fiercest blaze of all" is one Hebrew word, shalhevetyah: "flame" plus -yah, which may be Yah, short for God's name, its only trace in the Song. Many read it as a way of saying mightiest, as the BSB does; others hear a flame kindled by God.

layers.evidence: Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), Song of Songs: the oldest interpretation is allegorical; the Midrash and the Targum read it as the relations between God and Israel. Mishnah Yadayim 3:5, Rabbi Akiva (trans. Joshua Kulp, CC BY).
layers.text: Jewish readers long heard more than a love poem: the oldest readings take it as a picture of God and Israel. When rabbis debated which books were holy, Rabbi Akiva answered that all the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies.

The prophets already picture God as Israel's husband: "I will betroth you to Me forever," in "loving devotion"; "as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you"; "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride."

layers.evidence: Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), Song of Songs: the allegorical reading passed into the Church, as the relation between God or Jesus and the Church or the soul, elaborated by writers from Origen on.
layers.text: John the Baptist says, "The bride belongs to the bridegroom"; Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom; Paul applies marriage to "Christ and the church"; Revelation has "the marriage of the Lamb." Christians came to read the Song in this light.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Song 8:6 recalls Paul in Romans 8. Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: no waters can quench Christ's love to us.
layers.text: Christians hear in love "as strong as death" a love stronger still. Some recall Paul here: neither death nor life "will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Others add that no waters can quench Christ's love.

passages.saying: He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Isaiah sings about a vineyard its owner tended with every care, which still grew only sour grapes. Then he names it: the vineyard is Israel, and the fruit God wanted was justice.

The punchline is two pairs of sound-alike words: God looked for mishpat (justice) and found mispach (bloodshed), for tsedaqah (righteousness) and heard tse'aqah (a cry). Mispach occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, so its exact sense is not certain.

Tse'aqah is the cry God heard from the slaves in Egypt and the outcry against Sodom, and Isaiah has already called Jerusalem's rulers "rulers of Sodom." God's own people now cause the cry He once rescued them from.
Israel as God's vine is a running picture: "You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it."

Jesus retells this song as the parable of the tenants, with Isaiah's details: a planted vineyard, a wall, a wine vat, a watchtower. This time the owner sends his beloved son, and the leaders know the story is about them.
Jesus says, "I am the true vine." Where the vineyard of Isaiah 5 gave sour fruit, the true vine bears fruit, and those who remain in Him "bear much fruit."

passages.saying: If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, BDB, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." God sends Isaiah to say the invasion "will not happen." All turns on whether Ahaz will trust God, and he refuses even the sign God offers.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:9: a wordplay designed to draw attention to the alternatives set before the king; ta'aminu is the Hiphil and te'amenu the Niphal of aman. TBESH H0539: Niphal made firm, sure; Hiphil to trust, believe.
layers.text: The warning uses one Hebrew verb twice: im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu. Ta'aminu, "believe," and te'amenu, "be made firm," are two forms of aman. The pun sets the king's two choices side by side, and the BSB keeps the echo: "stand firm" and "stand at all."

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on 2 Chronicles 20:20: a play on believe and be established. Ellicott: an affirmative way of putting Isaiah's words to Ahaz. Keil and Delitzsch compare Isaiah 7:9.
layers.text: Earlier, King Jehoshaphat faced an invasion with the same pair: "Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld" (ha'aminu, te'amenu), Isaiah's warning put positively. His people sang, and "the LORD set ambushes" against the invaders.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: the first occurrence of H0539 is Genesis 15:6 (vehe'emin). BDB: to confirm, support, believe, trust.
layers.text: Aman first appears in the Bible when "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness," the verse Paul quotes in Romans and Galatians. Isaiah's pun shows what the word holds: in Hebrew, believing God and being made firm share one root.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Isaiah 28:16: ho pisteuōn ep' autō ou mē kataischynthē. TAHOT: ha-ma'amin is H0539.
layers.text: Isaiah's stone in Zion uses the word again: ha-ma'amin, "the one who believes will never be shaken." The Greek Old Testament reads "put to shame," and Paul and Peter quote it of Christ: "the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame."

layers.evidence: TBESG G0281: amen, from aman, be firm. The Cambridge Bible and Vincent: Isaiah 65:16 is literally the God of Amen. Pulpit Commentary: the faithful and true Witness amplifies the Amen.
layers.text: Amen comes from the same root, "be firm." Isaiah's "God of truth" is literally the God of Amen, and Jesus takes Amen as His title: "the Amen, the faithful and true Witness." So, Paul says, all God's promises are "Yes" in Christ.

passages.saying: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, David Kupp's and Markus Bockmuehl's work on Matthew, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." Isaiah offers him any sign he wants; Ahaz refuses to ask, so the Lord gives a sign anyway: a son to be called Immanuel.

layers.evidence: TBESH H6005: Immanuel, God with us. TAHOT writes the name as two words in 7:14 and 8:8, the same two words (H5973, H0410) that end 8:10.
layers.text: Immanuel is Hebrew for "God with us," as Matthew translates. Isaiah keeps sounding the name: the Assyrian flood will cover "your entire land, O Immanuel!" and the next oracle ends, "For God is with us," in Hebrew the same two words, immanu el.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary, giving Bishop Lowth's view: a double bearing and a double fulfillment. JFB: partly the immediate event, fully the Messiah. Gill: a sign of present deliverance. NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:14 and 7:16.
layers.text: The sign had a near horizon. Before the boy could "reject evil and choose good," the two kings' lands would be laid waste, and soon Assyria took Damascus. Isaiah's next son gets a similar timetable (8:4). So many readers see a double fulfillment, near and far.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible: almah strictly means a young woman of marriageable age. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G3933: parthenos renders almah at Genesis 24:43 and Isaiah 7:14. NET Bible notes: the word pertains to age; Matthew's parthenos shows he saw a virgin birth. Keil and Delitzsch; Gill.
layers.text: Matthew quotes this verse of Jesus' birth. Isaiah's word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and the Greek Old Testament had already rendered it parthenos, "virgin," here and for Rebekah in Genesis 24:43. What almah implies is still debated.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Ellicott on Isaiah 9:6: the name is applied to the LORD Himself in 10:21. Keil and Delitzsch: the same person as the son of the virgin in chapter 7. TAHOT: El Gibbor is H0410 and H1368 in both verses.
layers.text: Two chapters on, the child returns: "unto us a son is given," named "Mighty God," El Gibbor, who will "reign on the throne of David." A chapter later Isaiah uses El Gibbor of the LORD Himself: a remnant will return "to the Mighty God."

layers.evidence: David D. Kupp, Matthew's Emmanuel Messiah (PhD thesis, Durham, 1992), on the presence passages Matthew 1:23, 18:20 and 28:20. Markus Bockmuehl, Being Emmanuel, New Testament Studies 68.1 (2022).
layers.text: Matthew frames his Gospel with the name. It opens with "God with us" and ends with Jesus' last words: "surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age." In between He promises, "where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Hebrews 2:13: the words are from Isaiah 8:18, with Isaiah representing Christ. The Pulpit Commentary and the Cambridge Bible agree.
layers.text: Isaiah says he and his children are "signs and symbols in Israel," and Hebrews puts his words in Christ's mouth: "Here am I, and the children God has given Me." The prophet's sign-children become a picture of Christ and the family He brings to God.

passages.saying: He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Targum of Isaiah, and commentaries on Bible Hub.

layers.text: Isaiah describes the LORD's servant suffering for wrongs that are not His own. Watch the pronouns: the wounds are His, the transgressions are ours, and the peace and the healing come to us.

layers.evidence: Peter's word is molops, a bruise or wound left by a blow (TBESG, from Abbott-Smith). It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses here, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Isaiah's chabburah is a bruise or welt (TBESH). The link to the readers' beatings follows the Cambridge Bible, Pulpit and Ellicott on 1 Peter 2:24
layers.text: Peter quotes this line to household servants who could be beaten even for doing good: "By His stripes you are healed." Isaiah's "we" becomes "you," and Peter's word for stripes means a welt, a mark many of his readers knew on their own backs.

layers.evidence: Isaiah 53:4 has choli, sickness, and makob, pain (TBESH); the Greek Old Testament renders the first as sins. Matthew 8:17 follows the Hebrew. See the Expositor's Greek Testament, Barnes and Poole on Matthew 8:17
layers.text: The New Testament reads this song two ways at once. Matthew quotes 53:4 of Jesus' healings, where the Hebrew speaks of sickness. The Greek Old Testament made it sins, and Peter writes, "He Himself bore our sins." The Servant carries both.

"Crushed" is the Hebrew daka, and it returns five verses later: "it was the LORD’s will to crush Him." Onlookers thought God was striking Him (53:4). The chapter answers that He was crushed for our iniquities, and that even this served God's purpose.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible, Pulpit, Ellicott and Gill on Luke 22:37
layers.text: On His last night Jesus applies the chapter to Himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me," He says, and quotes 53:12, "He was numbered with the transgressors." The next day He was crucified between two criminals.

layers.evidence: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read the Servant as Israel. See Gill, Barnes and Ellicott on Acts 8:34
layers.text: An Ethiopian official asked, "who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?" Isaiah calls Israel God's servant (49:3), and medieval Jewish commentators read the song that way. Yet this Servant is "stricken for the transgression of My people." Philip answered with Jesus.

layers.evidence: Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 52:13 and 53:5 (English translation of 1871, on Sefaria). TBESH lists both senses of chalal, to pierce and to profane
layers.text: An early Jewish paraphrase in Aramaic, the Targum, names the Servant of 52:13 as the Messiah. In 53:5 it reads the word for "pierced" as "profaned" and applies it to the sanctuary. The Hebrew letters allow both senses.

passages.saying: I am watching over My word to accomplish it.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, BDB, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Young Jeremiah protests, "I am only a child!" God touches his mouth, puts His words there, and sends him "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant." Then He asks, "Jeremiah, what do you see?"

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Jeremiah 1:12: the almond blossoms in January or February and is the harbinger of spring. JFB: literally the wakeful tree. BDB on H8247: named for its early waking from winter's sleep.
layers.text: Jeremiah sees "a branch of an almond tree," shaqed, and God answers that He is shoqed, "watching." The almond is the first tree to blossom after winter, so its name means something like "the wakeful tree." God is awake over His word.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Amos 8:2: qets (end) sounds like qayits (summer fruit).
layers.text: Amos had a vision built the same way: "Amos, what do you see?" "A basket of summer fruit," qayits. Then God says the end, qets, "has come for My people Israel." Both visions turn an everyday object into a message through the sound of its name.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Jeremiah 31:28: the verb is the one in 1:12. Pulpit Commentary: an allusion to the twofold commission of 1:10. TAHOT: all three forms are H8245.
layers.text: The almond's verb returns beside the new-covenant promise: "Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down," so "I will watch over them to build and to plant," the two tasks of Jeremiah's call. God watches over rebuilding as He watched over judgment.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible on Hebrews 8:8: the quotation in Hebrews 8:8-12 is from Jeremiah 31:31-34.
layers.text: Three verses later comes what He is watching to build, "a new covenant": "I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts." Hebrews quotes the whole passage and says of Jesus, "the covenant He mediates is better."

passages.saying: And this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, BDB, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Judah's rulers have been shepherds who "destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture." God promises to "raise up for David a righteous Branch," a King who "will administer justice and righteousness in the land."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6667: Zedekiah, Jehovah is righteous, the last king of Judah, renamed from Mattaniah by Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott: the reigning king's name implied the same thought, and his reign was a miserable failure. Pulpit Commentary: it is singular that the name comes so near.
layers.text: Judah's last king was Zedekiah, a name the king of Babylon gave him, meaning the LORD is righteous. Yet "Zedekiah did evil in the sight of the LORD." He bore a name close to the promised one and failed it; the true King will be "The LORD Our Righteousness."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6780: a sprout or shoot, used of the Messiah from David's tree. BDB: a future ruler, pictured as a sprout from David's tree (compare Psalm 132:17).
layers.text: "Branch" is tsemach, a sprout: the future King springing from David's family tree. Jeremiah repeats it, "I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch," and after the exile Zechariah hears, "I am going to bring My servant, the Branch."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Jeremiah 33:16: there the title is given to the future King, here to the city. Gill and JFB: Christ and His church are one, so they share the name.
layers.text: When Jeremiah repeats the promise, the name moves from the King to His city: Jerusalem "will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." The King and His people share one name.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary: older Christian interpreters contended hard for the Messianic reading; Barnes and Poole see the King called Yahweh. Keil and Delitzsch: he by whom Jahveh deals righteousness, with the King's Godhead implicit in the name. Cambridge Bible: the prophet is not identifying the Messiah with Jehovah.
layers.text: Christians have long read the name of Christ, whom Paul calls "our righteousness," in whom "we might become the righteousness of God." Some hear the King called the LORD Himself; others, the one through whom the LORD gives righteousness.

passages.saying: I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, BDB, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea, explained as "four kings who will arise from the earth." Then the Ancient of Days takes His throne, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds and is given an everlasting kingdom.

layers.evidence: TBESH: bar, son; enash, man, human being. Keil and Delitzsch: like a man, not a beast; clouds are the chariot on which God comes to judge (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1).
layers.text: In Aramaic "son of man" is bar enash, simply a human being. After the beasts comes a human figure, yet he arrives with "the clouds of heaven," and in Scripture clouds carry God Himself: "the LORD rides on a swift cloud." Human, and coming as God comes.

layers.evidence: BDB on H6399: pay reverence to, serve (deity). All 10 biblical uses are religious, though later Aramaic (Targum Onkelos) also uses it of farm work. Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 28:18 ties the authority to Daniel 7:13-14.
layers.text: He is given a kingdom so "that the people of every nation and language should serve Him." The Bible uses this verb, pelach, only for religious service, as in "the God whom we serve." Jesus' last words echo the scene: all authority "has been given to Me."

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible and Gill on Mark 14:62 point to Daniel 7:13 and Psalm 110:1.
layers.text: Asked at His trial if He is the Christ, Jesus answers "I am," joining this verse to Psalm 110: "you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven." The high priest tears his clothes and cries blasphemy.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: the Son of Man occurs 80 times in the Gospels (NA28). TAHOT: ben adam occurs 94 times in Ezekiel. Barnes: the Saviour's favorite term for Himself.
layers.text: Son of Man was Jesus' favorite name for Himself, used about 80 times in the Gospels. It could sound humble: God calls Ezekiel "son of man" more than 90 times. But Jesus used it with authority: "the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch report Ibn Ezra (Aben Ezra) reading the figure as Israel; the Cambridge Bible: the ideal, glorified people of Israel. Gill: the Messiah, as most Christian interpreters allow.
layers.text: The angel's explanation shares the kingdom: "the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom." Some medieval Jewish and modern commentators read the figure as Israel; most Christian interpreters see the Messiah, who shares His kingdom with His people.

layers.evidence: Gill, the Cambridge Bible and Expositor's Greek Testament on Revelation 1:14: the description matches the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9.
layers.text: John sees "One like the Son of Man" whose hair is "white like wool, as white as snow," as Daniel described the Ancient of Days. The one who came to the throne shares the look of the One on it. And "He is coming with the clouds."

passages.saying: I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people,’ and they will say, ‘You are my God.’
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, BDB, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: God tells Hosea to marry an unfaithful wife, a living picture of Israel "departing from the LORD," and later to love her again, "as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods." Their children's names carry God's message.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Hosea 1:4: the massacre of Ahab's family by Jehu. NET Bible notes: yizre'el sounds like yisra'el. TBESH: Lo-ruhamah, no mercy; Lo-ammi, not my people.
layers.text: Each name is a sermon. Jezreel, which sounds like "Israel," recalls Jehu's massacre of Ahab's family there: "I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu." Lo-ruhamah means "no mercy," and Lo-ammi "not my people": "you are not My people."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Hosea 1:9: the Hebrew reads lo' 'ehyeh lakhem, I will not be yours; an allusion to Exodus 3:12, 14 and in effect a negation of it. TAHOT: all three are H1961.
layers.text: Literally, 1:9 ends with God saying He will not be (ehyeh) theirs. Ehyeh is the word God spoke at the burning bush: "I will surely be with you" and "I AM WHO I AM." Hosea's line turns that promise around.

layers.evidence: TBESH H3157: Jezreel, God sows; BDB: God soweth. Barnes: God changes the name's meaning to God shall sow. JFB: no longer God will scatter but God will plant.
layers.text: Then God turns the names inside out. Jezreel means "God sows," so the name of judgment becomes a harvest: the grain, wine and oil "will respond to Jezreel," and God says, "I will sow her as My own in the land." The God who scattered now plants.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: salvation is announced by simply turning the names into their opposites, dropping the lo (not). TAHOT: ammi (H5971) and ruhamah (H7355) in 2:1 and 2:23.
layers.text: The other two names simply lose their "not": "Say of your brothers, ‘My people,’ and of your sisters, ‘My loved one,’" in Hebrew ammi and ruhamah. Where they were told "You are not My people," "they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’"

layers.evidence: TBESH H5911: Achor, the valley of trouble where Achan was stoned; H5916 akhar, to trouble. Keil and Delitzsch: Joshua uses akhar for both Achan's sin and his punishment. NET Bible notes on Hosea 2:15.
layers.text: Even a place name is redeemed. The Valley of Achor, "trouble," was named for Achan's sin: "Why have you brought this trouble upon us?" Joshua asked. "Today the LORD will bring trouble upon you!" Now God will "make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope."

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Romans 9:25: first said of the return of the Ten Tribes; Paul is guided to expound it as a type of the bringing in of the Gentiles. Expositor's Greek Testament and Ellicott agree on the original sense.
layers.text: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes coming back to God. Paul applies his words to those God called "not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles," and Peter tells his readers, "Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God."

passages.saying: Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Jonah runs from God's call, is swallowed by a great fish, and finally preaches in Nineveh. The city repents and God spares it, to Jonah's anger.

layers.evidence: TBESH lists both senses of haphak
layers.text: "Overturned" is haphak, the verb used when God overthrew Sodom (BSB "destroyed"). But it can also mean to be turned or changed. Nineveh was overturned, just not as Jonah expected: it turned around.

The story moves step by step downward: Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into its hold, and down to the roots of the mountains, the same verb (yarad) each time, until God raises his life from the pit.

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH
layers.text: Jonah means "dove." Hosea calls the northern kingdom "a silly, senseless dove," and some readers see the runaway prophet as a picture of Israel itself.

Jesus names "the sign of the prophet Jonah": as Jonah was three days and three nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth. Nineveh repented, "and now One greater than Jonah is here."

Jonah sailed from Joppa to avoid preaching to Nineveh. Centuries later Peter, whom Jesus called "Simon son of Jonah" (John's Gospel has "son of John"), is staying in Joppa when God sends him to the Gentile Cornelius.

passages.saying: Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: The people complain, "Where is the God of justice?" God answers that He will send a messenger to clear the way, and then the Lord Himself will come to His temple, "like a refiner’s fire," to purify His people.

layers.evidence: TBESH H4401: Malachi, My messenger. JFB (Fausset) takes it as the name of an office, as the Septuagint of 1:1 (by the hand of his messenger) suggests; the Pulpit Commentary holds it is a proper name. Ellicott: the prophet chose the word with his own name in mind.
layers.text: The prophet's name, Malachi, means "My messenger," the very words of this verse. The word recurs: a priest "is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts." Some think Malachi is a title rather than a name; the Greek Old Testament of 1:1 has "his messenger."

layers.evidence: TBESH H4397: messenger, angel; TAHOT tags both messengers in 3:1 H4397. Ellicott: it must mean God Himself, since He comes to His temple; the Cambridge Bible, JFB and Pulpit agree.
layers.text: The verse has two messengers. The first prepares the way; the second, the "Messenger of the covenant," is "the Lord whom you seek" and comes "to His temple," His own house. Mal'akh means messenger or angel, and many read the second as God Himself arriving.

layers.evidence: Pulpit, Bengel and Ellicott on Matthew 11:10: Christ applies to Himself a prophecy of God's coming. The Septuagint of Exodus 23:20 and TAGNT of Matthew 11:10 share idou egō apostellō ton angelon mou pro prosōpou sou. NET Bible notes on Mark 1:2.
layers.text: Jesus applies the verse to John the Baptist with one change: "before Me" becomes "before You." The messenger prepares for God, and Jesus puts Himself in that place. His Greek opening matches Exodus 23:20 word for word: "I am sending an angel before you."

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible on Malachi 4:5: a first fulfilment in the Baptist, though by his own confession (John 1:21) he was not Elijah. JFB: an Elijah in spirit. Keil and Delitzsch: Elijah was sent in the person of John.
layers.text: Malachi names the messenger: "I will send you Elijah the prophet." John would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah," and Jesus calls him "the Elijah who was to come." Yet asked "Are you Elijah?", John said, "I am not": the role returned, not the man.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry and Keil and Delitzsch on Malachi 4:5: the close of Old Testament prophecy. Orthodox Bibles follow the Septuagint order and end the prophets with Daniel. NET Bible notes on Mark 1:2-3 and 1:6; Cambridge Bible on Mark 1:6 (2 Kings 1:8).
layers.text: Malachi closes the Old Testament in Protestant and Catholic Bibles, and Mark opens by quoting it with Isaiah's "voice of one calling." Then John appears dressed like Elijah, "with a leather belt around his waist." The story resumes where the prophets left off.

layers.evidence: Bengel on Matthew 17:3: both are named together in Malachi 4:4-5. Pulpit and Meyer: they represent the Law and the Prophets.
layers.text: Malachi's closing lines name Moses and Elijah together: "Remember the law of My servant Moses" and "I will send you Elijah the prophet." On the mountain of transfiguration those two appear, "talking with Jesus," the Law and the Prophets gathered around Him.

passages.saying: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TAHOT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Tertullian and John Chrysostom, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Near Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks, "Who do you say I am?" Simon Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus says this was revealed to him by His Father in heaven, and promises to build His church.

layers.evidence: Tertullian (Prescription Against Heretics 22) takes the rock as Peter; John Chrysostom (Homilies on Matthew 54) as the faith Peter confessed; Ellicott lists Peter's faith, the truth he confessed, or Christ. TBESG: petra is a mass of rock, petros a stone.
layers.text: Jesus puns on the name: "you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church." In Greek, Peter is Petros and rock is petra. What the rock is has long been debated: early Christian writers said Peter himself, or the faith he confessed; others say Christ.

layers.evidence: Ellicott: the two words were identical in the Aramaic Jesus probably spoke. The Expositor's Greek Testament gives the one Aramaic word, kepha; Bengel says the same of the Syriac. TBESG: Cephas is the Aramaic kepha, that is, Peter.
layers.text: Jesus probably spoke Aramaic, and John keeps Peter's Aramaic name, Cephas, "which is translated as Peter"; Paul uses it too. Kepha means rock, so in Aramaic the pun is exact: the same word twice.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary link the keys to Eliakim in Isaiah 22:22, and Ellicott to Revelation 3:7. Barnes: to bind was to forbid, to loose to allow; the Cambridge Bible cites the rabbinic schools of Shammai and Hillel binding and loosing.
layers.text: Jesus gives Peter "the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Isaiah's steward Eliakim was given "the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut," and Revelation gives it to Jesus. Binding and loosing were rabbis' words for forbidding and allowing.

layers.evidence: Ellicott finds the phrase in Hezekiah's song; the Cambridge Bible and the NET Bible note: Hades is the Hebrew Sheol. TBESG: in the Greek Old Testament hades chiefly renders Sheol, and pyle (gate) renders sha'ar. The NET Bible note: the gates of Hades may stand for the power of death.
layers.text: "The gates of Hades" is Old Testament language. Facing death, Hezekiah says, "I must go through the gates of Sheol," and God asks Job, "Have the gates of death been revealed to you?" Hades is Greek for Sheol. Death will not overpower what Jesus builds.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible on John 1:42 compare the renamings of Abram, Sarai and Jacob.
layers.text: God renames people at turning points: Abram becomes Abraham, "a father of many nations," and Jacob becomes Israel. On first meeting Simon, Jesus does the same: "You will be called Cephas." Older commentators compare these renamings.

passages.saying: Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TAHOT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, and Brandon Crowe's article in The Gospel Coalition.

layers.text: At night the disciples strain to row against the wind. In the fourth watch Jesus comes to them walking on the sea. They think He is a ghost and cry out, until He speaks, climbs into the boat, and the wind dies down.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) hears Job 9 in Mark 6:48. The Septuagint of Job 9:8 has peripaton epi thalasses, walking on the sea, as Mark has peripaton epi tes thalasses.
layers.text: In the Old Testament it is God who walks on the sea: "He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea." The Greek Old Testament has Him walking on the sea, in the words Mark uses when Jesus comes "walking on the sea."

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) links Exodus 33, 1 Kings 19 and Job 9. The NET Bible note gives both readings and cites Exodus 33:19, 22. The Septuagint has parerchomai, Mark's verb, in all three passages.
layers.text: "He intended to pass by them" recalls God passing by Moses and Elijah: "the LORD is about to pass by." Job says, "Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him." The Greek Old Testament uses Mark's verb in each. Others take it as how it looked to the disciples.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition): ego eimi could better be rendered I am, the language of the LORD's self-revelation. The Septuagint of Isaiah 43 has me phobou (do not fear) in verse 1, meta sou eimi in verse 2 and ego eimi in verse 10.
layers.text: "It is I" is ego eimi, literally "I am." It can be ordinary speech (the healed man says it in John 9:9), but here it may echo Isaiah 43, which pairs the same words in Greek too: "Do not fear," "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you," "I am He."

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (Westminster Theological Seminary, writing in The Gospel Coalition): the miracle anticipates the Transfiguration in Mark 9:2-8.
layers.text: The two men God "passed by" on His mountain were Moses and Elijah, and three chapters later they appear on another mountain, "talking with Jesus." One scholar reads the sea crossing as pointing ahead to that moment of glory.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) reads it as a new exodus led by the incarnate I am, citing Psalm 77:16-20 and Isaiah 43:16.
layers.text: Psalm 77 remembers the exodus: "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found." Isaiah's LORD "makes a way in the sea." Some read the night crossing as a new exodus, led by the "I am" Himself.

passages.saying: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Jesus ends His parable of the tenants, who kill the owner's beloved son, by quoting Psalm 118. The leaders understand that He told the parable against them.
In the psalm the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner: "This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes." The rejection is not the end; God reverses it.
Days earlier the crowds greeted Jesus with the same psalm: "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!" The week opens with one verse of Psalm 118 and turns on another.
In Hebrew "son" is ben and "stone" is even (eben). Some scholars suggest the parable's rejected son and the psalm's rejected stone are tied by this sound.

In Luke, Jesus adds that whoever falls on this stone will be broken and whoever it falls on will be crushed, drawing on Isaiah's "stone of stumbling" and Daniel's stone, cut without hands, that crushes the kingdoms and fills the earth.

The apostles keep building with this stone: Peter quotes it to the rulers and elders in Jerusalem, calls believers "living stones," and joins it to Isaiah's precious cornerstone, and Paul names Christ the cornerstone.

passages.saying: This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TAHOT, TBESG and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Reformation Study Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: At the Passover meal on His last night, Jesus breaks the bread, saying, "this is My body," then gives the cup: "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many." He explains His death before it happens.

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible on Mark 14:24 and Meyer on Matthew 26:28 trace the phrase to Exodus 24:8. TBESG: diatheke nearly always renders berit in the Greek Old Testament.
layers.text: Jesus takes up Moses' words at Sinai. Moses sprinkled blood on the people and said, "This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you." The first covenant was sealed in blood, and Hebrews quotes Moses' words as it explains the death of Christ.

layers.evidence: Gill: a feast was common at covenant making; Keil and Delitzsch see the Sinai meal as a type of the marriage supper of the Lamb. Ellicott links Mark 14:25 with Isaiah 25:6, and the Pulpit Commentary reads it as the marriage supper.
layers.text: At Sinai the covenant ended in a meal: the elders "saw the God of Israel," and "they ate and drank." Jesus seals His covenant at a table too, and looks ahead to drinking "anew in the kingdom of God," at Isaiah's feast where God "will swallow up death forever."

layers.evidence: In Mark 14:24 the most reliable manuscripts lack new (kaines), which other copies likely took from Luke 22:20 (NET Bible note; TAGNT). The NET Bible note: Jesus' death established the forgiveness promised in Jeremiah 31:31.
layers.text: Luke and Paul record "the new covenant in My blood," and Matthew adds "for the forgiveness of sins." Jeremiah had promised a new covenant written on the heart: "I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more."

layers.evidence: The Reformation Study Bible note on Mark 14:24: Jesus alludes to Isaiah 53:12. The echo of poured out is with the Hebrew, he'erah (TAHOT; TBESH); the Greek Old Testament shares only many.
layers.text: "Poured out for many" echoes Isaiah's suffering servant, who "poured out His life unto death" and "bore the sin of many." Jesus had already said He came "to give His life as a ransom for many."

layers.evidence: The Reformation Study Bible note on Mark 14:24 points to the Passover blood that protected Israel and the covenant blood of Exodus 24:8; the NET Bible note says Jesus is reinterpreting the Passover meal.
layers.text: It is Passover, "when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed." In Egypt the lamb's blood on the doorframes shielded Israel: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." At Sinai blood sealed the covenant. In this cup Jesus gathers both.

passages.saying: But when a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, he looked at him and had compassion.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, Thayer's lexicon, Augustine's Tractates on John, studies by F. Scott Spencer and Eben Scheffler, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: An expert in the law, "wanting to justify himself," asks Jesus, "And who is my neighbor?" Jesus tells of a man beaten on the road down to Jericho. A priest and a Levite pass by; a Samaritan stops, binds his wounds and pays for his care. "Go and do likewise."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Leviticus 19:34: the command to love your neighbor as yourself is here enacted for the stranger. Both verses use ve'ahavta (you shall love) and kamokha (as yourself) (TAHOT); a ger is a foreigner living in Israel (TBESH).
layers.text: The lawyer quotes Leviticus: "Love your neighbor as yourself," said there of "any of your people." Sixteen verses on it says of the foreigner living in Israel, "love him as yourself," in the same Hebrew. The law's love already reached past Israel's own people.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on 2 Chronicles 28:15 finds the likenesses curious, and Gill says these men of Samaria acted the good Samaritan. Studies: F. Scott Spencer, Westminster Theological Journal 46 (1984); Eben Scheffler, HTS Teologiese Studies 69 (2013).
layers.text: Some scholars hear an older story. In 2 Chronicles 28 men of Samaria, rebuked by a prophet, clothed their captives from Judah, "anointed their wounds, and put all the feeble on donkeys," and brought them to Jericho.

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible on Luke 10:33 links John 4:9 and Luke 9:53; Barnes calls the Samaritans the Jews' most bitter foes.
layers.text: Jews and Samaritans were bitter neighbors: "Jews do not associate with Samaritans." A chapter earlier a Samaritan village refused Jesus, and James and John wanted to "call down fire from heaven." Jesus rebuked them, then made a Samaritan the hero of His story.

layers.evidence: Thayer: to be moved in one's bowels, hence to have compassion. TAGNT has it in 12 verses, all in the first three Gospels: 8 of Jesus, 1 in a plea to Him (Mark 9:22), and 3 in parables.
layers.text: "Had compassion" is splanchnizomai, to be moved in one's inmost parts. The Gospels use it for Jesus, in a plea to Him, and in parables for the forgiving master, the father who runs to his lost son, and this Samaritan. The outsider feels what Jesus feels.

layers.evidence: Augustine, Tractates on John 43: Samaritan means keeper, and the Samaritan of the parable is our Keeper. TBESH: shamar, to keep or guard; Samaria, watch mountain.
layers.text: Opponents once called Jesus "a Samaritan," and He denied only the demon. An early Christian reading took Samaritan to mean keeper (from shamar, to keep) and saw the Lord in the Samaritan: "The LORD is your keeper," who "will neither slumber nor sleep."

passages.saying: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Asked for a sign in the temple courts, Jesus answers with a riddle. His hearers take Him to mean the temple building, which had taken 46 years to build.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) cites this passage for both senses of egeiro
layers.text: John explains: "Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body." The verb egeiro means both to raise a building and to raise the dead. The disciples understood only after the resurrection.

The misunderstood saying returns as a charge at His trial and a taunt at the cross: "You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days." The mockers are watching the first half come true.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG): in the Greek Old Testament this verb chiefly stands for shakan
layers.text: John has said the Word "made His dwelling among us." The verb comes from the word for a tent, and in the Greek Old Testament it chiefly stands for shakan, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt. Jesus' body is where God lives among His people.
The temple thread keeps widening: believers' bodies become "a temple of the Holy Spirit," and the new Jerusalem has no temple, "because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple."

passages.saying: Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born again, and Nicodemus asks how a grown man could enter his mother's womb a second time.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: anothen means both again and from above; Jesus' main sense is from above, and Nicodemus took it the other way. In John, TAGNT has anothen only at 3:3, 3:7, 3:31, 19:11 and 19:23.
layers.text: "Born again" uses anothen, which also means "from above." Nicodemus hears only a second birth, but elsewhere John uses the word for what comes from above: "The One who comes from above," authority "given to you from above," a tunic woven "from top to bottom."

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on John 3:8 points out the wordplay on wind and spirit. TBESG: pneuma is wind, breath or spirit.
layers.text: "The wind blows where it wishes," and "So it is with everyone born of the Spirit." Wind and Spirit are one Greek word, pneuma, and the saying turns on it: you hear the wind but do not know where it comes from, and so it is with the birth the Spirit gives.

layers.evidence: The Expositor's Greek Testament and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to Ezekiel 36:25-27. On the water, Barnes and Vincent see baptism, Poole the Spirit's cleansing, and the Expositor's Greek Testament a symbol.
layers.text: "Born of water and the Spirit" joins two promises God made through Ezekiel: "I will also sprinkle clean water on you" and "I will put My Spirit within you." So Jesus expects Israel's teacher to understand. Commentators still differ on what the water means.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on John 3:5 points to Ezekiel 37:9-10. TBESH: ruach is wind, breath, mind or spirit; TAHOT has it four times in Ezekiel 37:9.
layers.text: Hebrew has the same double word, ruach. In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones it is breath, wind and Spirit at once: "Come from the four winds, O breath," and "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live."

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on John 3:2 reads the timing as part of John's light and darkness theme, and says John probably had several meanings in mind.
layers.text: Nicodemus came "at night," and John recalls it when he brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial. The night likely fits John's theme of light and darkness: a man leaving the dark for the Light that "has come into the world."

passages.saying: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Jesus tells Nicodemus that, like the bronze snake Moses raised in the wilderness, He must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.
In Numbers the people speak against God, venomous snakes bite them, and God tells Moses to make a snake and set it on a pole. Moses makes it of bronze, and whoever is bitten and looks at it lives.
In Hebrew, snake is nachash and bronze is nechoshet, so the "bronze snake" is a nechash nechoshet: the two words sound almost alike.

"Lifted up" (hypsoo) means raised up and also exalted. When Jesus says it again, John adds that it showed "the kind of death He was going to die," and Acts uses the same verb for His exaltation to God's right hand. The cross is His lifting up.

Isaiah's suffering servant "will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted," just before the description of His suffering. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb there, and many scholars think John's "lifted up" draws on this verse.

layers.evidence: Meaning of nechoshet from TBESH
layers.text: Centuries later Israel was burning incense to that same bronze snake, now called Nehushtan, a name built on nechoshet, "bronze," and King Hezekiah smashed it. The sign had become an idol; the healing never lay in the bronze.

passages.saying: you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah, older commentaries named under each note, and articles by Carissa Quinn (BibleProject) and Jennifer Garcia Bashaw.

layers.text: Weary from His journey, Jesus sits by Jacob's well in Samaria and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. She asks how a Jew can ask her. He offers her living water instead, "a fount of water springing up to eternal life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the word translated living is used in Greek of flowing water. Abbott-Smith (TBESG): springing as opposed to still water; Meyer: spring water as opposed to water in a cistern.
layers.text: In Greek, "living water" meant flowing water, from a spring rather than a cistern. So she asks how He will draw it, since "the well is deep." She hears spring water; Jesus means water that wells up to eternal life.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: mayim chayyim in Genesis 26:19 and Jeremiah 2:13, and the same chayyim in the cleansing law of Leviticus 14:5 (BSB fresh water there too). TBESH: chay is living, and of water, flowing or fresh. Meyer cites Jeremiah 2:13.
layers.text: Hebrew says the same, mayim chayyim. Isaac's servants find "a well of fresh water" (literally living water), and Jeremiah gives the phrase to God: "They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns."

layers.evidence: Carissa Quinn (BibleProject) and Jennifer Garcia Bashaw (Working Preacher), after Robert Alter's biblical type-scenes; Bashaw suggests this betrothal scene is of the Samaritans to their God.
layers.text: A man meets a woman at a well, and a marriage follows: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah, Jacob meets Rachel, Moses meets Zipporah. This is "Jacob’s well," a chapter after John the Baptist calls Jesus "the bridegroom." This time many in her town believe.

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 describes water drawn from the Siloam pool in a golden jug and poured at the altar. The NET Bible note on John 7:38: Jesus takes up the water of the ceremony and uses it figuratively.
layers.text: At the Feast of Tabernacles, when by Jewish tradition water from Siloam was poured at the altar, Jesus promises "streams of living water," meaning the Spirit. Zechariah's vision of living water from Jerusalem ends with the nations keeping that feast.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: a question opened with me in Greek expects the answer no. Bengel and the Cambridge Bible compare John 8:53; the Pulpit Commentary finds her words possibly ironic.
layers.text: She asks, "Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well?" In Greek the question expects the answer no, but John's readers know better. Jesus meets the same question about Abraham, and the Samaritans end up calling Him "the Savior of the world."

passages.saying: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: The day after feeding five thousand, Jesus tells the crowd that He Himself is the bread that satisfies: whoever comes to Him will never hunger.

The crowd asks for a sign like the manna and quotes Scripture: "He gave them bread from heaven to eat," words close to Exodus 16:4 and Psalm 78:24. Jesus answers that the true bread from heaven comes from His Father, and unlike the manna, whoever eats it will not die.
Manna is named after a question. When Israel first saw it they asked one another, "What is it?" (man hu), and they called it man. Moses answered, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat."

Moses said the manna taught Israel that "man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD." Jesus quotes this in the wilderness, and in John the Word made flesh is Himself the bread.
John notes that Passover was near. The bread Jesus will give "for the life of the world" is His flesh, which many readers connect with the Last Supper: "This is My body, given for you."

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH
layers.text: Jesus was born in Bethlehem, whose name means "house of bread," and was laid in a manger, a feeding trough. Christians have long noticed the Bread of Life coming from the House of Bread; the Gospels do not point it out.

passages.saying: Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, BDB, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah, Irenaeus and Augustine, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused it; Jesus says neither: it happened "so that the works of God would be displayed in him." He makes mud, puts it on the man's eyes and sends him to wash. He comes back seeing.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the Hebrew name shiloah comes from the verb to send, though BDB calls the link uncertain. Augustine, Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible and the Pulpit Commentary see Jesus as the one Sent. John's word for Sent is a form of apostello, the verb of John 17:3 and 20:21 (TAGNT).
layers.text: John stops to translate the pool's name: Siloam, Isaiah's "Shiloah," means "Sent." In John, Jesus is the Sent One, doing "the works of Him who sent Me." So a man sent to the pool called Sent is healed by the One sent from God.

layers.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.15.2: the clay points to how man was first fashioned and shows the hand of God that formed him from the dust. The Greek pelos (clay) occurs in the New Testament only in John 9 and Romans 9:21 (TAGNT).
layers.text: Only here in the Gospels does Jesus make mud to heal. An early Christian reading sees the Creator's hand: as God formed man "from the dust of the ground," so Jesus used clay on the eyes, showing how humanity was first made. John himself does not say this.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Isaiah 42:7: the Messiah would cure blindness of body and of spirit. The Expositor's Greek Testament and Meyer hear Isaiah 35:5 in Matthew 11:5. Isaiah 35:5 and 42:7 share the verb paqach (open) and the noun ivver (blind) (TAHOT).
layers.text: "Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind." Yet Isaiah promised that "the eyes of the blind will be opened," and that God's servant would open them. Asked by John the Baptist, Jesus points to such signs: "The blind receive sight."

layers.evidence: Meyer and the Cambridge Bible cite Isaiah 6:9-10, which John quotes in 12:40. The NET Bible note calls the man's worship the climax of the story.
layers.text: The sign becomes a two-edged saying: "so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind." The man goes from "The man they call Jesus" to "a prophet" to worship, while leaders who "claim you can see" stay blind. John later ties this to Isaiah.

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 (water from Siloam poured at the altar) and 5:3 (every courtyard in Jerusalem lit), written down later. The NET Bible note and Vincent also link Siloam's water to the feast.
layers.text: This follows the Feast of Tabernacles, where Jesus said, "I am the light of the world." Later Jewish writings say that feast drew water from Siloam for the altar and lit every courtyard in Jerusalem. Now the Light of the world sends a blind man there.

passages.saying: Lazarus, come out!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Genesis Rabbah, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: When His friend Lazarus falls sick, Jesus waits two days, saying the sickness is "for the glory of God." He arrives when Lazarus has been four days in the tomb, tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life," and calls the dead man out.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (TBESG): a colloquial short form of Eleazar; TBESH: Eleazar means God has helped. Ellicott on Luke 16:20 thinks the name may picture the beggar's helplessness; the Expositor's Greek Testament says no symbolic meaning should be attached.
layers.text: Lazarus is a short form of Eleazar, a Hebrew name meaning "God has helped." John never comments on the name. For Luke's beggar, some commentators think it may picture a man who had no other help; others see no symbolism.

layers.evidence: Bengel, Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible and Alford (quoted by Vincent) on Luke 16:31 note the match.
layers.text: In a parable in Luke, Jesus names a beggar Lazarus, and the story ends, "they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead." In John a man named Lazarus rises, and the chief priests plan "to kill Lazarus as well." The Gospels never link the two.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: Caiaphas meant political expediency, and John reads his words in a sense Caiaphas could not have imagined.
layers.text: Caiaphas argues, "it is better for you that one man die for the people." He means politics, but John says that as high priest he "was prophesying" that Jesus would die for the nation and for "the scattered children of God." One sentence, two meanings.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 11:43 point to John 5:25 and 5:28-29. The same noun, phone (voice), is in John 11:43 and 5:28 (TAGNT).
layers.text: Jesus had said that "all who are in their graves will hear His voice" and come out. At Bethany one grave hears that voice early: "The man who had been dead came out." It is a near, partial fulfillment of a far promise.

layers.evidence: Genesis Rabbah 100:7 (Bar Kappara); Gill and the Expositor's Greek Testament cite the tradition. Barnes: the delay rules out deception or a mere swoon.
layers.text: John mentions the four days twice, and Martha warns, "by now he stinks." A rabbinic saying, written down later, held that the soul stays near the grave for three days. After four days, commentators note, no one could say Lazarus had only seemed dead.

passages.saying: God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: At Pentecost Peter tells the crowd that Jesus died "by God’s set plan and foreknowledge," but God raised Him. Death had seized Him but could not keep Him: "it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches."

layers.evidence: Ellicott: literally travail-pangs. TBESH lists chevel, a cord, and chevel, pain or travail. The Septuagint of Psalm 18:4 has odines thanatou, as in Acts 2:24; Meyer calls that rendering an error.
layers.text: The word behind "agony" is odines, labor pains. It echoes the Psalms: "The cords of death encompassed me." In Hebrew chevel means a cord, and a word with the same letters means a labor pain. The Greek Old Testament took it the second way, in Luke's very words.
