layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary: loosed applies better to cords than to pangs. Meyer reads the resurrection as a birth from the dead; Vincent finds that far-fetched. The Septuagint of Psalm 18:5 renders the cords of Sheol as odines hadou.
layers.text: Both senses fit. The verb for "releasing" is lyo, to untie, which suits cords better than pains: God loosed "the cords of Sheol." Some also hear a birth: death went into labor and could not hold what it bore.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Colossians 1:18, citing Acts 2:24: He comes out from the dead as the firstborn from the womb. Ellicott calls the resurrection His second birth; also Meyer and Poole. Others read firstborn as rank, and TBESG files it under priority.
layers.text: Many hear the same picture in a title Paul and John both give Jesus: "firstborn from among the dead" and "the firstborn from the dead." Older commentators call the resurrection His second birth, coming out of the grave as a child comes from the womb.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 16:21: the figure was often used by the prophets (Isaiah 21:3, 26:17-18, 66:7-8). Isaiah 26:17 has chevel, pain (TAHOT); in 26:19 the verb for bring forth can mean give birth (NET Bible note).
layers.text: Jesus pictured the grief of His death and the joy of Easter as childbirth: the mother "forgets her anguish," and "I will see you again." Isaiah 26 uses the same picture: labor pains give way to "Your dead will live" and "the earth will bring forth her dead."

passages.saying: they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Paul warns the Corinthians not to presume on their privileges: Israel was rescued, fed and given water in the wilderness, and still most of them fell.
Twice God gave water from a rock. At Horeb Moses was told to strike it; years later he was told to speak to it, struck it twice instead, and was barred from the land.

Moses named the place Massah (testing) and Meribah (quarreling) because the people asked, "Is the LORD among us or not?" Psalm 95 keeps the names as a warning, and Hebrews, quoting the psalm in Greek, gives their meanings: "in the rebellion, in the day of testing."

In the Song of Moses, Rock is a name for God: "He is the Rock, His work is perfect." Paul echoes that song twice in this chapter (sacrifices to demons, provoking God to jealousy), so "that rock was Christ" puts Christ in the place of Israel's God.
Paul names his way of reading: these things happened "as examples" and "were written down as warnings for us." The Greek words are typoi and typikos, where the word "type" comes from.
Jesus calls out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink." Some readers also connect the struck rock with Christ pierced on the cross, when "blood and water flowed out" from His side.

passages.saying: Death has been swallowed up in victory.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, BDB, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Paul ends his chapter on the resurrection with a mystery: "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed." At the last trumpet the dead will rise imperishable, and then the saying will come true: "Death has been swallowed up in victory."

layers.evidence: NET Bible note on Isaiah 25:8: in Canaanite thought death was a hungry enemy swallowing its victims. Vincent and the Expositor's Greek Testament: the Septuagint has death prevailing and swallowing men up, and Paul follows the Hebrew. TBESG: katapino renders bala.
layers.text: Paul quotes Isaiah's promise of a banquet "for all the peoples," where "He will swallow up death forever." Death was pictured as a hungry enemy swallowing its victims; here God swallows death. The common Greek version reversed it, so Paul follows the Hebrew.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible: a kindred word in Syriac and Aramaic means victory; BDB gives netsach no victory sense. TBESG lists Septuagint renderings of netsach as eis nikos, including 2 Samuel 2:26. The Expositor's Greek Testament: Theodotion's Greek matches Paul's wording.
layers.text: Isaiah's "forever" is netsach, which in Hebrew means perpetuity. A related Aramaic word means victory, so Greek translators often wrote "to victory," even in "Must the sword devour forever?" With that echo, one word holds both promises: forever, and victory.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the opening lines may be questions implying no rescue, Death and Sheol are invited to come, and the last line means no compassion for Israel; the Expositor's Greek Testament gives both readings. Where the Septuagint of Hosea has dike (penalty), Paul has nikos, victory (TBESG).
layers.text: Paul echoes Hosea: "Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?" Readers differ on Hosea's tone: a promise of rescue, or God calling death against Israel, for the verse ends "Compassion is hidden from My eyes." Paul makes it a taunt.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Barnes, Vincent and the Pulpit Commentary on Revelation 21:4 point back to Isaiah 25:8; Revelation 7:17 repeats the promise.
layers.text: Isaiah's verse goes on: "The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face." Paul takes the first half and John the second: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes," and "there will be no more death." One promise ends both death and tears.

layers.evidence: TBESG: katapino is the Septuagint's usual word for bala, swallow, as in Isaiah 25:8. Ellicott, Meyer and Vincent on 2 Corinthians 5:4 compare 1 Corinthians 15:54.
layers.text: Paul uses the picture again: in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed, "so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life." The Greek verb is the same, katapino. Death used to do the swallowing. Now life does.

passages.saying: If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Didache (Lightfoot's translation), articles by David Capes and Michael Bird, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The Greek text spells out the Aramaic marana tha (NET Bible note).
layers.text: Paul takes the pen to write the closing greeting in his own hand. Then come a warning and a prayer: "If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!" The prayer is in Aramaic, not Greek: marana tha.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note and the Cambridge Bible give both readings. TAGNT: NA28, NA27 and SBL print marana tha; Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text print maran atha.
layers.text: The Aramaic divides two ways. Marana tha (Our Lord, come!) is a prayer; maran atha (our Lord has come, or is coming) is a confession. Printed Greek texts divide it both ways. Both are true of Jesus: He came, and He is coming.

layers.evidence: Vincent: the reason for the Aramaic is unknown. David Capes, following Larry Hurtado: the Aramaic for Lord (mare', TBESH) could be a divine title. Michael Bird: Jesus was made the object of prayer in worship, though that alone does not identify Him as Israel's God.
layers.text: Why Aramaic in a letter to Greeks? No one knows for sure, but many scholars hear a prayer of the first church in Judea, which called Jesus maran, our Lord, a title that could also be used of God. In their worship, Jesus was the one they prayed to.

layers.evidence: Didache 10.6, in J. B. Lightfoot's translation. Vincent on 1 Corinthians 16:22 notes the link, and Michael Bird reads the prayer as looking to the Lord's coming.
layers.text: The Didache, an early Christian writing, ends its prayer after the Lord's Supper the same way, asking for grace to come and this world to pass away, then maran atha. Paul ties the Supper to the same hope: "you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes."

layers.evidence: Vincent on 1 Corinthians 16:22 compares Revelation 22:20, as does David Capes. Barnes: John answers in the very words the Savior had used.
layers.text: The Bible's last book closes with the same prayer in Greek. Jesus says, "Yes, I am coming soon," and John answers in His own words, "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!" Paul's Aramaic prayer and John's Greek one ask for the same thing.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Galatians 4:6: Christ's own cry becomes the believers' cry. TBESG: abba is Aramaic for father.
layers.text: Paul's Greek letters keep another Aramaic prayer word, Abba. Jesus prayed "Abba, Father" in Gethsemane, and the Spirit of the Son in our hearts cries "Abba, Father!" So Paul's letters keep two Aramaic prayers: Abba to the Father, and marana tha to the Son.

passages.saying: we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Biblical Archaeology Review, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Paul compares two ministries. At Sinai the Israelites "could not gaze at the face of Moses," and he veiled it. In Christ the veil is gone: believers "with unveiled faces" reflect the Lord's glory and are being changed into His image.

layers.evidence: Meyer: Exodus gives no express word that the glow faded; the Pulpit Commentary: Paul seizes on a point Exodus does not dwell on. The Hebrew for this veil, masveh, occurs only in Exodus 34:33-35 (TAHOT).
layers.text: Paul is retelling Exodus 34. Moses came down Sinai "unaware that his face had become radiant," and after speaking to the people "he put a veil over his face." Exodus never says the glow faded; that detail is Paul's own reading.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: qaran comes from qeren in the sense of a ray of light; Aquila's Greek and the Vulgate give horns. Gill: the Septuagint says his face was glorified. Lee M. Jefferson (Biblical Archaeology Review 49:1, 2023): Jerome wrote cornuta esset facies, and the history of the horns is complicated.
layers.text: The word for "radiant," qaran, comes from qeren, a horn or a ray (Habakkuk 3:4). The Greek Old Testament says his face was glorified, and Paul calls it glory. The Latin Bible said horned, and Michelangelo's Moses has horns, though the history is complex.

layers.evidence: Cambridge Bible: a quotation of the Septuagint of Exodus 34:34, with the tense changed; the Expositor's Greek Testament and Bengel call it a paraphrase. Both have henika (whenever), periaireo (remove) and kalymma (veil).
layers.text: Exodus says that whenever Moses went in before the LORD, "he would remove the veil." Paul reworks it, keeping its Greek words for whenever, remove and veil: "whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away." What Moses alone did, anyone may now do.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible: the same verb as the Transfiguration. It occurs only in Matthew 17:2, Mark 9:2, Romans 12:2 and here (TAGNT; TBESG).
layers.text: The word for "transformed" is metamorphoo, used when Jesus "was transfigured" and "His face shone like the sun." Its only other use is "be transformed by the renewing of your mind." Moses' face shone, Jesus' face shone, and now believers are being changed.

layers.evidence: TBESG: to reflect as a mirror; TAGNT: beholding as in a mirror. Beholding: Meyer, Barnes, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary. Reflecting: the Expositor's Greek Testament, MacLaren, the Cambridge Bible.
layers.text: The verb for "reflect," katoptrizomai, comes from the word for a mirror. It can mean to reflect like a mirror or to look as into a mirror, and commentators split between the two. Moses did both: he met the LORD face to face, and his face shone.

layers.evidence: The Expositor's Greek Testament calls the words a paraphrase of Genesis 1:3, and Meyer and Ellicott agree; Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown link the face of Jesus to the face of Moses.
layers.text: Paul goes back to creation: the God who said "Let light shine out of darkness" now gives "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." The face that shone at Sinai pointed to this face: Christ, "the image of God."

passages.saying: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: To teach humility, Paul tells Christ's story. Existing "in the form of God," He "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant," and became obedient to death on a cross. So God gave Him "the name above all names," before which every knee will bow.

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible calls it an implicit citation of Isaiah 45:23 and a powerful witness to Paul's view of Jesus' deity; Barnes, Meyer and the Pulpit Commentary also hear Isaiah 45:23.
layers.text: Paul's words come from Isaiah 45, where the LORD swears by Himself: "Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance." He has just said, "I am God, and there is no other." Paul applies the LORD's own oath to Jesus.

layers.evidence: TBESG: kampto (bow) and exomologeo (confess) in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10-11, from the Septuagint of Isaiah 45:23, whose printed editions vary between confess and swear. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Cambridge Bible note Romans 14:11.
layers.text: In Romans Paul quotes the same verse about God's judgment: "every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God." In Philippians the same bowing and confessing, in the same Greek verbs, happen at the name of Jesus, "to the glory of God the Father."

layers.evidence: TBESG: kyrios chiefly renders YHWH in the Septuagint. The Cambridge Bible (the Lord, Jehovah), the Expositor's Greek Testament and the Pulpit Commentary (Lord, or Jehovah) and Ellicott (Jehovah) read God's own name; Meyer takes it as Jesus Christ, and Gill also disagrees.
layers.text: Which is "the name above all names"? Many older commentators answer: Lord, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God's own name, YHWH. Others disagree. Isaiah's speaker is "I, the LORD," and now every tongue confesses "that Jesus Christ is Lord."

layers.evidence: The Expositor's Greek Testament: the Lord, Jehovah in Joel, is here plainly Christ, which shows how fully Christ stands in God's place in salvation; Ellicott, Meyer and Barnes agree.
layers.text: Paul does the same with Joel. Joel's promise, "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved," uses God's own name, YHWH. Romans quotes it soon after "if you confess with your mouth" that "Jesus is Lord," so the Lord to call on is Jesus.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary reads Christ here as the Servant of the LORD; the Expositor's Greek Testament reports Taylor's comparison of Philippians 2:7-9 with Isaiah 52:13 and 53:12; Gill notes Christ was foretold as a servant.
layers.text: The story follows Isaiah's suffering Servant. Christ takes "the form of a servant," is "obedient to death," and God exalts Him to the highest place. The Servant "will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted," because "He has poured out His life unto death."

layers.evidence: Matthew Poole and Gill contrast the sin of Adam and Eve; Bengel cites Genesis 3:5. Harpagmos (grasped) comes from harpazo, to seize, and its exact sense is disputed (TBESG).
layers.text: Some readers also hear Adam. The serpent promised, "you will be like God," and our first parents reached for it. Christ, though "in the form of God," "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped." It is an echo, not a quotation.

passages.saying: First, his name means “king of righteousness.” Then also, “king of Salem” means “king of peace.”
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Hebrews argues that Jesus is a priest of a different and permanent kind, not from Levi's family but "in the order of Melchizedek," who "always lives to intercede."

Genesis gives Melchizedek three verses: king of Salem and "priest of God Most High," he brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth from him. The only other Old Testament verse to name him is Psalm 110:4.
Later, in Psalm 110, God swears to David's Lord: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." Hebrews builds its argument on this oath.

layers.evidence: Name meanings, and the note on Jewish commentators, from TBESH
layers.text: Hebrews reads the names. Melchizedek joins melek (king) and tsedeq (righteousness), and Salem means peace. The Old Testament names Salem only once more, in Psalm 76:2, in parallel with Zion, and most Jewish commentators identify it with Jerusalem.
Jesus Himself raised Psalm 110 in the temple: David calls the Messiah "my Lord." The psalm that seats the Messiah at God's right hand also makes Him a priest forever.
Genesis records no father, mother, birth or death for Melchizedek, and Hebrews makes the silence part of the picture: "like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time."
Many Christian writers link Melchizedek's bread and wine to the bread and cup of the Last Supper. Hebrews does not mention it.

passages.saying: In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the Online Etymology Dictionary, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Hebrews explains why Christ had to die. He is "the mediator of a new covenant," so that the called may receive "the promised eternal inheritance." And an inheritance comes through a death: "a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died."

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (TBESG): diatheke nearly always renders berit in the Septuagint, but in classical Greek means a will. The Cambridge Bible and the Expositor's Greek Testament see a play on the double meaning, and Meyer reads will in 9:16-17; Vincent and Ellicott read covenant throughout.
layers.text: One Greek word, diatheke, is "covenant" in verse 15 and "a will" in verses 16-17. In the Greek Old Testament it nearly always stands for berit, covenant, but in everyday Greek it meant a will. Many hear a play on both senses; some read "covenant" throughout.

layers.evidence: Vincent: the Vulgate has testamentum even where covenant is beyond doubt; Online Etymology Dictionary: Late Latin vetus and novum testamentum translate the Greek. Barnes: the only place Scripture calls the Jewish books the old covenant; the Cambridge Bible: the books of Moses read in the synagogue.
layers.text: This double word named the Bible's two halves. Latin rendered diatheke as testamentum, a will, even where it meant covenant, so the covenants became the Old and New Testaments. Paul once says "the old covenant," for the books of Moses read in the synagogue.

layers.evidence: Bequest: the Cambridge Bible, and Bengel, who calls it a word fit for one dying. Covenant: Ellicott and Barnes. Abbott-Smith (TBESG) glosses the verb here as to assign.
layers.text: At the Last Supper Jesus says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood," and then, "I bestow on you a kingdom," with diatithemi, the verb behind diatheke. Some hear a bequest, as if on His last night Jesus were making His will; others hear covenant language.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary: the expression comes from Isaiah 63:11, where the Septuagint has ton poimena ton probaton, and the covenant blood from Zechariah 9:11. Also the Cambridge Bible, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ellicott and Meyer.
layers.text: Hebrews closes by naming the God who,"through the blood of the eternal covenant," raised "that great Shepherd of the sheep." The Greek of Isaiah 63:11 gives Moses, brought up from the sea, the same title, and Zechariah speaks of "the blood of My covenant."

passages.saying: Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, the Online Etymology Dictionary, Peter Leithart and G. K. Beale, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: John greets the seven churches with grace and peace from God, from the seven Spirits, and from Jesus, named three ways: witness, firstborn, ruler. Then he breaks into praise: "To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood."

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale, as reported by Peter Leithart (Theopolis Institute, 2011): all three phrases are in Psalm 89:27 and 37. The Septuagint of 89:37 has martys and pistos, witness and faithful; the Cambridge Bible and Ellicott also cite the psalm.
layers.text: All three titles come from Psalm 89, God's oath to David's heir: "I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth," and his throne will last like the moon, "a faithful witness in the sky."

layers.evidence: Peter Leithart (Theopolis Institute, 2011): the psalm asks but never answers, and Revelation is about the faithfulness of Israel's God to Israel's King.
layers.text: Psalm 89 then turns to grief: "You have renounced the covenant with Your servant," and "Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old?" The psalm never answers. Some read Revelation as the answer: David's heir is alive and reigning.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the word can mean both witness and martyr; Online Etymology Dictionary on martyr. The Pulpit Commentary: the same Greek phrase is used of Antipas and of Christ.
layers.text: The Greek for "witness," martys, can also mean martyr, and gave English that word. Jesus gives His own title to a believer who died for Him: "My faithful witness Antipas was killed among you." Antipas shares his Lord's title, and his Lord's death.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the two oldest manuscripts read freed; the NET Bible note gives it better manuscript support. TAGNT: lousanti in the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text. MacLaren: washed pictures sin as a stain, loosed as a chain.
layers.text: Copies differ here by one letter. The oldest read lysanti, "released"; others read lousanti, "washed." One pictures sin as a chain, the other as a stain. Revelation knows both: the saints "have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."

layers.evidence: MacLaren calls Exodus 19:6 the charter of Israel's national life, given right after the exodus. Peter's royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9) follows the Septuagint of the same verse (Ellicott, Meyer, the Pulpit Commentary).
layers.text: The words "a kingdom, priests" come from Sinai, just after the exodus: "you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." John keeps Israel's order: first freed, then made priests. Heaven sings, "You have made them to be a kingdom and priests."

passages.saying: all its dimensions were equal—12,000 stadia in length and width and height.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, G. K. Beale's work, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: a stade was about 607 feet (185 m).
layers.text: An angel shows John "the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God" and measures it with a golden rod. Its length, width and height are equal, 12,000 stadia each: a cube about 1,400 miles (2,200 km) on a side.

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale (Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48, 2005): the city is cubic because only the Holy of Holies was a cube (1 Kings 6:20). Also the Pulpit Commentary and Vincent.
layers.text: The shape points to one room, the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple: "twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high," overlaid with pure gold. The city is pure gold too. The holiest room has become the whole city.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: dwelling place, traditionally tabernacle, literally tent. The Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott and Gill link Ezekiel 37:27 and Leviticus 26:11-12, given on Mount Sinai (Leviticus 26:46).
layers.text: The voice from the throne explains: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them." The word is skene, a tent or tabernacle. It fulfills God's promise at Sinai, "I will make My dwelling place among you," repeated in Ezekiel.

layers.evidence: The Cambridge Bible and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Ezekiel 48:35 point ahead to Revelation 21:3.
layers.text: Ezekiel's vision of the restored city ends with its name: "from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE," in Hebrew YHWH shammah. The new Jerusalem is the city whose very name is God's presence.

layers.evidence: The Expositor's Greek Testament: the names show continuity with God's ancient people. The Cambridge Bible and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compare Ezekiel 48:30-35; Bengel links Hebrews 11:10 with Revelation 21:14.
layers.text: Like Ezekiel's city, its gates bear "the names of the twelve tribes of Israel," and its foundations "the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb": one people of God. It is "the city with foundations" Abraham awaited, "whose architect and builder is God."

layers.evidence: The Septuagint of Exodus 28:17-20 shares eight names with Revelation 21:19-20: jasper, sapphire, emerald, sardius, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, amethyst. Ellicott notes the order differs; Gill and Benson see an allusion. The Cambridge Bible warns against finding symbolism in every detail.
layers.text: The foundations are "adorned with every kind of precious stone," as Isaiah promised. The high priest wore twelve stones for the tribes, and eight of John's twelve are on the Greek Old Testament's list, in another order. Some warn against pressing the details.

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale (Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48, 2005): all God's people will have become high priests. MacLaren and Gill also see the high priest's plate here.
layers.text: Only the high priest wore God's name on his forehead, on a gold plate engraved "HOLY TO THE LORD." In the city every servant of God bears it: "His name will be on their foreheads." What one man wore before the LORD, all His people now wear.

passages.saying: On either side of the river stood a tree of life
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: John's last vision shows a river of life flowing from God's throne through the new Jerusalem, with the tree of life on both banks and its leaves "for the healing of the nations."

The Bible ends where it began. Eden had a river and the tree of life; after the fall the way to that tree was guarded. Now it stands open: "Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life."
The picture also comes from Ezekiel's vision of water flowing from the temple, with fruit trees on both banks that bear every month and leaves for healing.

"No longer will there be any curse" answers the curse on the ground in Genesis 3 and echoes Zechariah's promise that Jerusalem would never again be under the ban (cherem, which BSB renders "utter destruction").

"They will see His face." Adam and Eve hid from God's presence, and Moses was told no one can see God's face and live. Jesus promised that the pure in heart will see God. At the end, what was lost and forbidden is given.
"The Lord God will shine on them" takes up Isaiah's promise: "the LORD will be your everlasting light."
